upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the peace with God the sword was never aimed at. Human loyalties realign and households crack; the reconciliation Christ won between you and the Father stands underneath the division, the deeper peace the blade clears ground for and never touches.
reflection: Where has following Christ divided me from people I love, and have I read it as my failure?
Which old loyalty has my new allegiance reordered, and who feels the floor shifting?
Can I hold the grief of the sword and still trust the deeper peace it clears ground for?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, the sword has fallen where I least wanted it, between me and people I love, and I have wondered if I failed. You named it before it came so I would not mistake it for Your absence. Hold me in the grief, and root me in the deeper peace with God that the blade was never aimed against. Amen.

notes.primary: Matthew 10:34 (not peace but a sword); Luke 12:51 (division, not peace).

title: Not my will
moment: The deepest disconnect in Scripture happens on the ground, in a garden, in the dark. He kneels among the olive trees, and the sweat comes down like falling blood, and He prays the most human prayer there is: Father, if you are willing, take this cup from me. He does not want it. He says so plainly, and He says it more than once. There is no pretending here, no manufactured calm. He asks for the cup to pass because He honestly wishes it would. And then, in the same breath, He makes the break that every other break in the world only rehearses. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done. He hands over the one thing a person clings to hardest — the wanting itself, the preference, the plan — while the wanting is still alive and aching in His chest. To surrender your own will, not after it has gone quiet but while it is still crying out, is the hardest rupture a human heart can make. He made it first. He made it in the dark, on the ground, and He made it for us.
voiceQuote: Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.
scriptureText: My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me; nevertheless, not what I want, but what you want.
weight: The break God asks of you may not be from a possession or a place or a person. It may be from your own will — the plan you have built your hope on, the preference you cannot seem to lay down, the outcome you are still aching for in the middle of the night. We imagine surrender as a kind of peace that descends and quiets the wanting first. Gethsemane says otherwise. You can want the cup gone with your whole body and still pray that His will be done. The honesty and the obedience are not enemies; they belong together on the same ground. You do not have to feel serene to be faithful, and you do not have to stop wishing for another way in order to say yours be done. The raw asking is not a failure of trust. It is what real surrender looks like before it is finished — a heart that tells God the truth about what it wants, and hands the wanting over anyway.

upheaval.thePhase: This is Disconnect at its most interior: the break not from something you hold but from your own will. The phase asks what every garden asks — that you release your grip on the outcome while the longing for it is still raw, praying not my will but yours, and meaning it without pretending the cup is easy.
upheaval.inYou: The break before you may not be from a possession or a place or a person. It may be from your own will, the plan you built your hope on, the preference you cannot lay down, the outcome you are still aching for in the middle of the night. Gethsemane shows you can want the cup gone with your whole body and still pray that His will be done; the honesty and the obedience are not enemies but belong on the same ground. You do not have to feel serene to be faithful, nor stop wishing for another way to say yours be done. Tell God the truth about what you want, and hand the wanting over in the same prayer, while it is still aching in your chest.
upheaval.inTheBody: The Church, too, is sometimes asked to break from its own will, its preferred future, its institutional self-interest, the survival instinct that can masquerade as faithfulness. Across history the Body has faced moments where obedience plainly cost it power, property, or standing before a watching world, where the will of God ran straight against the will to self-preservation. The Gethsemane prayer, prayed by the whole Church, is costly beyond measure: not our will but yours, even when Christianity can see exactly what that obedience will cost and chooses it anyway. The temptation is always to grasp the cup of safety while still mouthing the words of surrender. The Church that means the prayer lets its own preference go, the longing for it still raw.
upheaval.whatRemains: When your own will is finally broken, what does not break is the Father into whose hands the will is given. The wanting can be shaken loose; His good purpose underneath it cannot. That is what remains when surrender has cost you everything — not your plan, but the One who held you while you let it go.
reflection: What cup am I still asking God to take from me, and can I pray yours be done in the same breath?
Where have I mistaken raw honesty about my wants for a lack of faith?
What would it look like to hand over my own will while it is still aching, rather than waiting to feel calm first?
upheaval.prayer: Father, there is a cup I do not want, and I will not pretend otherwise. I have asked You to take it, and I ask again. And still, in the same breath, I give You my will: not what I want, but what You want. Hold me while I let it go. Amen.

notes.primary: Luke 22:42 / Matthew 26:39 (not my will but yours, in Gethsemane).

title: It is finished
moment: The cross is the ultimate disconnect, and it speaks two words that should not be able to live in the same hour. The first is desolation. Out of the darkness over the whole land comes the most forsaken cry ever uttered: my God, my God, why have you forsaken me. The communion at the very center of reality — the Son with the Father, before all worlds — seems, for one unbearable moment, to tear. There is no softening this. He is not performing abandonment; He is in it. And then, from the same cross, in the same dying, comes the other word, and it is not a word of defeat. It is finished. Not I am finished, not it is over and lost, but the work is done, accomplished, complete. The thing He came to do has been carried all the way through to the end. So the deepest rupture the universe has ever known is, at the very same instant, its deepest completion. The tearing and the finishing are one act. What looks from below like the end of everything is, from the cross itself, the accomplishing of everything.
voiceQuote: When Jesus had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished. He bowed his head, and gave up his spirit.
scriptureText: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?
weight: When your own forsakenness is at its worst — when God seems to have torn Himself away and left you alone in the dark, when the prayers go up and nothing comes back down — the cross does not hand you an explanation. It hands you a companion. Even that desolation has been entered, borne all the way to the bottom, and turned into finished work. There is no abandonment you can feel that He has not already felt ahead of you. He went into the God-forsaken dark first, and He came out the other side calling it accomplished. So when you cannot sense Him, the question is not whether He is real but whether your feeling is the final word. It is not. The cross says the worst hour you will ever live was walked through by the Son, and on its far side stands a word you cannot yet say but He has already spoken over it: finished. The dark is not the end of the story. It is finished is.

upheaval.thePhase: This is Disconnect at its furthest reach — the Son forsaken, the rupture total. Yet the phase reveals its secret here: the very same break is the work completed. Disconnect asks you to trust that even the bottom, even the dark where God seems gone, can be the place where something is finished rather than the place where you are.
upheaval.inYou: When you feel most God-forsaken, torn from, left in the dark, sure He has gone and the prayers go up and nothing comes back down, the cross does not hand you an explanation. It hands you a companion. Even that desolation has been entered, borne all the way to the bottom, and turned into finished work. There is no abandonment you can feel that He has not felt ahead of you; He went into the God-forsaken dark first and came out calling it accomplished. So when you cannot sense Him, the question is not whether He is real but whether your feeling is the final word. It is not. Your dark is not the end of your story; the word He finished over the worst hour, it is done, is.
upheaval.inTheBody: The Church has known hours that felt like outright forsakenness, seasons when whole Christian civilizations collapsed and the Body was stripped of everything it leaned on while the heavens went silent. Yet the cross stands at the very center of the faith precisely as the disconnect that accomplished everything, the rupture that was also the completion. So the Church in its darkest passages has not fallen out of the story of its Lord; it is walking the shape He walked first. Forsakenness, public and total, is no more the end of the Body than it was the end of the Son. From the far side of the worst the Church will ever endure, the word already spoken over it is not defeat but the same finished work.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the finished work itself. Feelings of abandonment come and go; the cry in the dark is real and then it passes. But what was accomplished on that cross is done, and nothing can undo it. When everything else is torn away, the completed work of Christ remains, finished and unshakable.
reflection: Where do I feel most forsaken right now, and have I let that feeling become the final word?
Can I believe that Christ has already walked through the exact dark I am in?
What changes if the worst hour of my life is met not by an explanation but by a finished work?
upheaval.prayer: Lord Jesus, in the dark I have wondered if You forsook me. You know that cry; You made it first. Thank You that even my forsakenness has been entered and borne by You. When I cannot feel You, hold me to the word You finished over it: it is done. Amen.

notes.primary: John 19:30 (it is finished); Matthew 27:46 (my God, my God, why have you forsaken me).

title: The veil is torn
moment: At the very moment He dies, something tears in a building across the city. The veil of the temple, the thick curtain that walled off the holiest place, rips in two from top to bottom. The direction matters. It is not torn from the bottom up, as if human hands had finally reached high enough to pull it down. It tears from the top, from God's end, His doing and not ours. For generations that curtain had done its work, keeping everyone out of the place where God was said to dwell, admitting only one man one day a year, and only with blood. Now, in an instant, it hangs open. This is disconnect as doorway. The whole old system of separation comes to an end, and through the very place it tears, a new and living way opens straight into the presence no one could approach before. Hebrews would later say the way leads through the veil, that is, through His flesh — the curtain and the body torn in the same hour, for the same reason. Sometimes the breaking of the old order is the exact thing that grants an access no one ever had while it stood.
voiceQuote: The veil of the temple was torn in two from the top to the bottom.
voiceAttribution: Mark, at the moment of Jesus' death — Mark 15:38 (WEB)
scriptureText: a new and living way, which he dedicated for us, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh.
weight: The breaking in your life may be the tearing of a veil. We assume that what is old and familiar is therefore safe, that the long-standing thing must be the protecting thing. But some of what hangs in our lives, for all its familiarity, has been quietly keeping us at a distance — a structure, a habit of religion, a way of relating to God that felt reverent and was really just a wall. When it tears, the first feeling is loss. Something that always hung there is suddenly in pieces. Yet ask the harder question: was it keeping you near, or keeping you out? Not every barrier that falls is a tragedy. The torn veil teaches that God will sometimes rip the old wide open precisely to grant the nearness it was blocking. What feels like the rending of something sacred can turn out to be the opening of a way you could never have reached while the old thing still hung intact between you and Him.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect is not only loss; here it is doorway. The phase asks you to read the tearing rightly — to see that when an old order ends, the rending itself may be the opening of a way. What looks like pure destruction from one side is, from God's side, access granted. The break is the door.
upheaval.inYou: The breaking in your life may be the tearing of a veil. We assume that what is old and familiar is therefore safe, that the long-standing thing must be the protecting thing. But some of what hangs in your life, for all its familiarity, has been quietly keeping you at a distance, a structure, a habit of religion, a way of relating to God that felt reverent and was really just a wall. When it tears, the first feeling is loss. Ask the harder question: was it keeping you near, or keeping you out? What feels like the rending of something sacred can be the opening of a way you could never reach while the old thing still hung intact between you and Him.
upheaval.inTheBody: When the old structures of the Church tear, the honest question is whether a veil has just been removed. Much that the Body has clung to as sacred, layers of mediation, hardened hierarchies, the long accretions that put distance between ordinary people and God, was quietly keeping the many out of the holy place while everyone called it reverence. The Reformation's recovery of direct access, and every later upheaval that stripped away what walled people off from Christ, can look from one side like pure destruction and from God's side like access granted. The torn veil is the pattern over the whole Church: the LORD will sometimes rip an old order wide open, top to bottom and by His own hand, to grant the very nearness it had been blocking.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the access itself — the new and living way opened through the torn veil. Curtains and structures can be rent; the open road into God's presence cannot be closed again. When the old barriers fall, what remains is nearer than the barriers ever let you come: the way standing open.
reflection: What in my life that has torn might actually have been a veil keeping me at a distance?
Where have I mistaken a wall for something sacred simply because it was familiar?
Am I grieving a barrier God tore down to bring me nearer than it ever allowed?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, You tore the veil from the top, with Your own hand, to open the way to Yourself. When the old things in my life tear, give me eyes to see whether You are removing a wall that kept me distant. Lead me through the torn veil into the nearness I could never reach before. Amen.

notes.primary: Mark 15:38 (the veil torn top to bottom); Hebrews 10:20 (a new and living way through the veil).

title: The look that found Peter
moment: Not every disconnect is one we choose nobly. Some are the breaks of our own failing, and this is one of the hardest in the Gospels. Peter, who had sworn he never would, who had drawn a sword for his Lord only hours before, now stands in a courtyard by a charcoal fire and denies Him. Once. Twice. A third time, with cursing. And just then the cock crows, and across the courtyard the Lord turns and looks at him. Luke does not tell us it was a glare. He tells us only that He looked. In that look is everything Peter has done and everything Peter still is to Him, held together at once. And Peter remembers the word that had named this very hour, and he goes out, and he weeps bitterly. There it is — the most devastating break a person can know, the one we cause ourselves, the failure we were certain we would never commit. And the look that finds us inside it is not the end of hope. For Peter, across the dark days ahead, that look was the beginning of grace, not its closing.
voiceQuote: The Lord turned, and looked at Peter.
scriptureText: He went out, and wept bitterly.
weight: Maybe the rupture you are living was your own doing — a denial, a betrayal, a collapse you swore you would never be capable of, and then were. There is a particular agony in the breaks we cannot blame on anyone else. The self-inflicted wound carries its own voice, and the voice says: this one disqualifies you, this is where it ends. The courtyard says no. The Lord turned and looked at Peter, and the look did not finish him; it found him. The bitter weeping that follows is not the sound of a door closing. For Peter it was the doorway back — the grief that grace uses to bring a man home. Your failure is real, and naming it honestly matters; this is no airbrushing of sin. But a self-inflicted break is not the final word over your life. The same Lord who looked across that fire knows exactly what you did, and turns toward you still. That turning is where restoration begins.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect includes the breaks we cause ourselves — not the noble rupture but the shameful one. The phase asks something hard here: to let the failure be real without letting it be final, and to receive the look that finds you in it. The break of your own making is still a break God can meet, and even use.
upheaval.inYou: Maybe the rupture you are living was your own doing, a denial, a betrayal, a collapse you swore you would never be capable of, and then were. There is a particular agony in the breaks we cannot blame on anyone else; the self-inflicted wound carries its own voice, and the voice says this one disqualifies you. The courtyard says no. The Lord turned and looked at Peter, and the look did not finish him; it found him. The bitter weeping that follows is not a door closing. For Peter it was the doorway back, the grief grace uses to bring a person home. Your failure is real, but it is not the final word, and the same Lord who knows exactly what you did turns toward you still.
upheaval.inTheBody: The Church has broken faith with its Lord again and again, denied Him in cowardice when confession was costly, failed Him in public scandal before a watching world, and wept about it only later. Peter in the courtyard is the Body's own story, not a single failure but a recurring one across the centuries. Yet the look that finds the failing Church is not first condemnation; it is the turning of a Lord whose own faithfulness never gave way when His people's did. The bitter reckoning the Church is driven to after its denials has, again and again, become the doorway back rather than the door closing. A Christianity that has denied its Lord in some dark courtyard is not therefore finished with Him, nor He with it.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the Lord's turning toward you in the failure. Your faithfulness gave way; His did not. The look across the fire holds both the truth of what you did and the welcome still extended. When your own collapse has shaken everything, His unbroken grace toward you remains.
reflection: What self-inflicted break am I treating as the end of my story?
Can I believe the Lord's look finds me rather than only condemns me?
Where is bitter weeping over my own failure being made into a doorway back?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, the worst break in my life is the one I caused — I denied what I swore I would defend, and I know it. You turned and looked at Peter, and the look was grace. Turn toward me now. Let my weeping be the doorway back, and begin in me the restoration only You can. Amen.

notes.primary: Luke 22:61-62 (the Lord looked at Peter; he wept bitterly).

title: Saul on the road
moment: Saul is riding hard for Damascus, arrest warrants folded in his bag, when the light throws him to the ground. He had been the most zealous defender of the old order alive, certain to his bones that he was serving God by hunting down the followers of the Way. And out of the light comes a voice that names him and undoes him in the same word: Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me. Me. The One he thought he was defending God against is the One he has been wounding. In a single instant the whole framework he had built his life upon lies in pieces in the dust, and the man who arrived as the persecutor cannot even see; they have to lead him by the hand into the city. For three days he sits blind in the dark. Then Ananias comes, and something like scales falls from his eyes, and he can see, and he rises and is baptized. The break of conversion can be exactly this violent — a life cut cleanly in two, a before and an after with a flash of light between them, the persecutor unmade so that the apostle can be born.
voiceQuote: He fell on the earth, and heard a voice saying to him, Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?
voiceAttribution: Luke, of Saul on the Damascus road — Acts 9:4 (WEB)
scriptureText: Immediately there fell from his eyes as it were scales, and he received his sight; and he arose and was baptized.
weight: God sometimes interrupts a life mid-stride, hard enough to put a person flat on the ground in the road. We picture conversion and renewal as gentle, a slow warming, a quiet turning. Sometimes it is. But sometimes it is a light that knocks you down and takes your sight and leaves you groping in the dark for three days, no longer sure of the one thing you were surest of. If your upheaval did that to you — if it cut your life cleanly into before and after and left you blind for a stretch — you are in old and good company. Do not despair of the blindness. Saul did not arrange the scales to fall; he sat in the dark and waited, and in their own time they fell. The violence of the break is not a sign that God has abandoned you to it. For the man on the Damascus road, being struck down was the beginning of seeing, and the blindness was never meant to last.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect can come as violent conversion — not a gradual turning but a life cut cleanly in two. The phase asks you to let the old framework lie broken in the dust rather than scrambling to reassemble it, and to sit in the blindness in trust. The break that knocks you flat may be the very thing clearing your eyes.
upheaval.inYou: God sometimes interrupts a life mid-stride, hard enough to put a person flat on the ground in the road. We picture conversion and renewal as gentle, a slow warming, a quiet turning, and sometimes it is. But sometimes it is a light that knocks you down, takes your sight, and leaves you groping in the dark for three days, no longer sure of the one thing you were surest of. If your upheaval did that, if it cut your life cleanly into a before and an after, you are in old and good company. Do not despair of the blindness. Saul did not arrange the scales to fall; he waited, and in their own time they fell. The break that felled you was the beginning of seeing.
upheaval.inTheBody: The Church's fiercest opponents have become its greatest apostles, and the Body has never been allowed to forget it. The man who held the coats at a stoning and went house to house to drag believers out became the missionary who carried the gospel across the empire. No movement, no nation, no hostile age is beyond the Damascus break, and the whole Church is meant to hold that stubborn hope even for the powers persecuting Christianity now. The God who stopped Saul on the road still turns enemies of the faith into builders of the very thing they set out to destroy. The Body prays for its persecutors because it has watched, across two thousand years, the persecutor become the apostle more than once.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the Lord who meets us on the road. Frameworks shatter, certainties collapse, sight itself can be taken for a time. But the voice that named Saul holds steady through all of it. When your whole world has been cut in two, the One who stopped you on the road remains, and He is not done with you.
reflection: Where has an upheaval cut my life cleanly into a before and an after?
Am I scrambling to rebuild an old framework God has let fall to pieces in the dust?
Can I sit in the blindness and trust that the scales will fall in their own time?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, You stopped Saul on the road and undid him to remake him. If You have knocked me flat and taken my sight for a season, help me not to despair of the dark. I will wait for the scales to fall. Let the break that felled me be the beginning of seeing. Amen.

notes.primary: Acts 9:4, 18 (Saul struck down on the road; scales fall from his eyes).

title: Counted as loss
moment: Years after the road to Damascus, Paul sits down and does the arithmetic of his own life out loud. He had a ledger any devout man would envy: circumcised on the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, a Pharisee, blameless under the law, the kind of pedigree that opened every door and silenced every doubt. All of it once sat in the gain column, totaled and proud. Then he draws a line through the page. Whatever things were gain to him, he says, these he has counted loss for Christ. He does not stop there. Beside the surpassing worth of knowing Jesus, the whole impressive sum is refuse — the word is blunt, the word for garbage, for what you scrape off and throw out. Notice he is not confessing that his credentials were sins. They were real assets, hard-won and genuine. He is saying they were the wrong currency. Set next to Christ they would not even spend. So he reckons them up one last time and deliberately moves the entire balance across the page, from gain to loss, eyes open, on purpose.
voiceQuote: What things were gain to me, these have I counted loss for Christ.
scriptureText: I count all things to be loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord... and count them but refuse, that I may gain Christ.
weight: The break sometimes comes for the very things you have banked your identity on. Not your obvious failures, those are easy to disown, but your achievements, the credentials you were proudest of, the record you would hand anyone who asked who you are. An upheaval can ask you to recount all of it and write the word loss beside the line that used to read gain. This is not self-hatred, and it is not pretending the achievements never happened. It is honest re-pricing. The things you are being asked to release were real, but they were never worth what He is, and the moment you set them beside Him the difference is plain. A divided ledger keeps you wealthy and unfree, your worth scattered across a dozen assets that an upheaval can liquidate in an afternoon. The clean accounting Paul models is the freer one: count it loss, call it what it is, and quit defending a net worth that was never the point. What looks like a write-off is the beginning of true gain.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect, here, is the break made on purpose and with open eyes. It does not wait for crisis to strip you; it asks you to do the stripping yourself, to recount the old credentials and deliberately reckon them loss. The phase demands a clear-eyed re-pricing of everything you have called gain, and the courage to move the balance across the page.
upheaval.inYou: Your upheaval may come not for your obvious failures, which are easy enough to disown, but for the very things you have banked your identity on, the credentials you were proudest of, the record you would hand anyone who asked who you are. It can ask you to recount all of it and write the word loss beside the line that used to read gain. This is not self-hatred, and it is not pretending the achievements never happened. It is honest re-pricing. What you are being asked to release was real, but it was never worth what He is, and beside Him the difference is plain. A divided ledger keeps you wealthy and unfree; call it loss, and quit defending a net worth that was never the point.
upheaval.inTheBody: The Church can grow rich in the wrong currency, banking on its prestige, its reputation, its inherited pedigree and institutional gains as though these were the treasure. Whole traditions have mistaken cultural dominance, magnificent buildings, and political standing for spiritual wealth, and defended that net worth fiercely while growing poor toward God. The Body that can sit down and do the honest arithmetic, recounting its assets and naming the idols among them as refuse, is free to gain Christ in a way the self-impressed Church never can. The surpassing worth of knowing Him does not show up in a proud ledger. Across history, the renewals that mattered began where Christianity moved its whole impressive balance, eyes open, from the gain column to loss.
upheaval.whatRemains: When every credential is reckoned loss, what is left in the gain column cannot be shaken: the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus. Every other asset can be liquidated by an upheaval. He cannot. He is the one possession no write-off touches and no reversal undoes.
reflection: What have I quietly banked my identity on that an upheaval could liquidate in an afternoon?
Which of my gains am I afraid to recount, because I suspect Christ would price them differently?
Am I willing to call my proudest credentials loss, not because they were sins, but because He is worth more?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have kept a proud ledger and counted as gain what was never the treasure. Teach me the honest arithmetic Paul made. Help me reckon my credentials loss beside the surpassing worth of knowing You, and to do it with open eyes, gladly, for I would gain Christ. Amen.

notes.primary: Philippians 3:7-8 (what was gain, counted loss; all things refuse to gain Christ).

title: Sent out from Antioch
moment: At Antioch the break turns corporate and outward. This is no failing church being disciplined; it is one of the healthiest congregations in the world, gifted, multiethnic, well taught, the very place where believers were first called Christians. Its leaders are worshiping and fasting when the Holy Spirit speaks into the room: set apart Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them. Read that slowly. Of all the things the Spirit might ask of a thriving church, He asks for its two best men. Barnabas, the bridge-builder, the one who first vouched for the dangerous convert. Saul, the towering teacher. The Spirit does not request the spare capacity or the surplus. He asks the church to disconnect itself from its finest leaders and launch them toward a horizon no one can see. So they fast and pray, lay hands on the two, and send them away. The verb is plain and costly. They sent them away, out of the warmth of the center, into the unknown. Mission begins, as it almost always does, with a sending that takes something real from the ones who send.
voiceQuote: As they served the Lord and fasted, the Holy Spirit said, Separate Barnabas and Saul for me, for the work to which I have called them.
voiceAttribution: Luke, of the church at Antioch — Acts 13:2 (WEB)
scriptureText: When they had fasted and prayed and laid their hands on them, they sent them away.
weight: Sometimes the break is not something done to you and not something you choose against the body; it is the body choosing, under God, to break a piece of itself off and let it go. And that hurts on both sides of the laying-on of hands. To be sent is to be pried loose from people you love and a place that formed you, set apart for a work somewhere else, and it can feel like loss to everyone in the room. It is loss. It is also obedience. The deeper temptation is the church's, not the sent one's: to keep the best where they are useful and safe, to call hoarding stewardship, to mistake a full and impressive center for health. But a body that will not release its strongest cannot multiply; it can only accumulate. The Spirit still walks into the worship of thriving churches and asks for their finest. The sending costs exactly what it looks like it costs, and the cost is the point.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect is not always a rupture forced by crisis; sometimes it is the deliberate, outward break of a healthy body sending its best away from the center. The phase asks a thriving community to loosen its grip on its own strength, to lay hands on its finest and let them go, and to feel the real cost of obedience without calling it loss alone.
upheaval.inYou: Sometimes the break is being sent, pried loose from a place that formed you and people you love, set apart for a work somewhere else. Do not be surprised that it aches; being sent can feel like loss to everyone in the room, and it is. It is also obedience. The Spirit still says, separate this one for the work I have called him to, and the calling does not stop because it costs you the leaving. You will be tempted to read the grief as proof you have misheard. You have not. The warmth of the center was never meant to be a cage. To be launched toward an unseen horizon is loss and obedience at once, and the cost is part of the shape of the call.
upheaval.inTheBody: The Church is meant to be a sending Body, and its deepest temptation is to keep its best where they are useful and safe, to call hoarding stewardship, to mistake a full and impressive center for health. Antioch sets the pattern for the whole Church: a thriving fellowship laying hands on its two finest leaders and launching them toward an unseen horizon, feeling the real cost and obeying anyway. Across the centuries the Body has multiplied only where it was willing to release its strongest into the unknown rather than accumulate them at home. The Church that clings to its own strength grows heavier where it stands; the Christianity that sends pieces of itself away, against every instinct to hold them, is the one the Spirit spreads across the world.
upheaval.whatRemains: When a church sends its best into the unknown, it can let go because the One sending them is unshakable. The center may feel thinner; the Lord of the harvest does not. What cannot be shaken is His command and His keeping, holding both the sent and the sending church when the warm familiar circle is broken open.
reflection: What strength am I holding safe at the center, calling it stewardship when it is really hoarding?
If the Spirit asked for my finest, the people or gifts I most rely on, could I lay hands on them and let go?
Have I treated being sent, or sending, as pure loss, when the cost was the very shape of obedience?
upheaval.prayer: Lord of the harvest, You ask thriving churches for their best and send them into the unknown. Loosen my grip on the strength I keep safe at the center. Make me willing to lay hands and let go, to be sent or to send, trusting the cost is not loss but obedience. Amen.

notes.primary: Acts 13:2-3 (the Spirit sets apart Barnabas and Saul; they are sent out).

title: What God has cleansed
moment: Peter's break is interior and seismic, and it begins on a rooftop at noon, hungry, while lunch is being made below. He falls into a trance and sees the sky open, a great sheet let down by its corners, and in it every kind of creature his Scriptures had taught him to refuse. A voice says, rise, kill, and eat. He recoils on reflex: never, Lord, I have never eaten anything common or unclean. And the answer overturns a lifetime in a single sentence. What God has cleansed, do not call unholy. Three times the vision comes, until the refusal itself is pried out of his hands. He is being disconnected from categories he had always assumed were not opinions but God's own boundaries, the very architecture of holy and profane. While he is still turning it over, men arrive from a Roman centurion's house, and the meaning lands. The sheet was never really about food. By the time he stands in the home of Cornelius, a Gentile, on the far side of a wall he had never once thought to question, the wall is already down, and Peter says it plainly: I truly perceive that God shows no partiality.
voiceQuote: What God has cleansed, you must not make unholy.
scriptureText: Truly I perceive that God doesn't show favoritism.
weight: The hardest break is not always the loss of something you loved. Sometimes it is the falling of a boundary you were certain God Himself had drawn. Those breaks cut deeper than grief, because they cut into certainty. You can grieve a loss and still know which way is up; but when the line you policed as sacred turns out to be a line God is erasing, the floor of your confidence tilts. Peter does not get there by argument; he gets there by a vision repeated until his reflex gives way and then by watching God pour out the same Spirit on the wrong people. The discipline this asks of you is severe and rare: to hold even your boundaries with an open hand, to keep asking whether the thing you have been confidently calling unclean is something God has already cleansed. Not every line dissolves; the LORD draws real ones. But when an upheaval runs straight to the border of your certainty, it is worth wondering who is doing the erasing.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect here is the break from old boundaries, the falling of categories you held as sacred. This is the most disorienting form of the phase, because it severs not a comfort but a certainty. It asks you to loosen your grip on the very lines you assumed were God's own, and to let Him cleanse what you have been confident to call unclean.
upheaval.inYou: God may be dismantling a boundary you have held as holy, a category of people, a rule, a line you were sure He Himself had drawn. These breaks cut deeper than grief, because they cut into certainty; when the line you policed as sacred turns out to be one God is erasing, the floor of your confidence tilts. Peter did not get there by argument but by a vision repeated until his reflex gave way. When the break runs to the borders of your certainty, do not assume the certainty is God. Ask whether the LORD is cleansing the very thing you have called unclean, and whether your refusal is reflex rather than faith. Not every line dissolves; He draws real ones. But wonder who is doing the erasing.
upheaval.inTheBody: The Church's great breaks have often been the falling of walls it assumed were divine. The Gentile question came first, the staggering discovery that God showed no partiality and had cleansed what the people of God were certain was unclean. Walls have fallen since that the Body policed as the LORD's own, only to find Him already standing on the other side. This is the most disorienting upheaval the Church can pass through, because it severs not a comfort but a certainty. The whole Church is called to hold even its boundaries humbly, remembering that the LORD reserves the right to cleanse what His reluctant people have called unholy. A Christianity that guards its lines as if God needed defending keeps finding Him out ahead, tearing the very walls down.
upheaval.whatRemains: When the boundaries you trusted come down, the God behind them does not. His impartial mercy was the deeper truth the wall obscured. What cannot be shaken is His own holiness and His freedom to cleanse, the LORD who shows no partiality, standing firm precisely where our certainties give way.
reflection: What boundary have I policed as sacred that God may be quietly erasing?
Is my refusal of someone or something faith, or only reflex dressed as conviction?
Where might God already be standing on the other side of a wall I assumed was His?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have called some lines Your own that were only mine, and policed them as if You needed defending. Where You are cleansing what I have called unclean, soften my reflex and open my hand. Teach me to follow You past the walls You are tearing down. Amen.

notes.primary: Acts 10:15, 34 (what God has cleansed; God shows no partiality).

title: Scattered, and preaching
moment: Not every disconnect is chosen; some are inflicted from outside, by people who mean only to destroy. On the day Stephen is buried, a great persecution erupts against the church in Jerusalem, and a young man named Saul goes house to house, dragging out men and women. The community that had been so visibly one, breaking bread together and holding everything in common, is broken apart and driven from the city, scattered through the regions of Judea and Samaria, all of them except the apostles. Read it as the persecutors did and it is a victory: the troublesome sect dispersed, its center emptied, its people running for their lives. It looks like pure catastrophe, the church shattered and homeless. And then comes the line that turns the whole scene inside out. Those who were scattered abroad went around preaching the word. The very dispersion meant to extinguish the gospel carried it everywhere, like seed flung off a threshing floor by a wind that thought it was scattering chaff. What broke the church apart is precisely what planted it across the world. The catastrophe was the sowing.
voiceQuote: Those who were scattered abroad went around preaching the word.
voiceAttribution: Luke, of the scattered church — Acts 8:4 (WEB)
scriptureText: A great persecution arose against the assembly which was in Jerusalem, and they were all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except for the apostles.
weight: The break you did not choose is not outside God's reach, and it is not outside His habit. The job lost, the community fractured, the displacement forced on you by someone else's decision or someone else's cruelty, all of it can feel like wind tearing through a life that was finally settled. And settled is often exactly the problem. The Jerusalem church had everything good and was going nowhere, gathered tightly in one city while a whole world waited. It took a storm to do what comfort never would. This does not make the persecution good; it was evil, and God does not need to be thanked for the cruelty to be trusted with the outcome. But He has a long, documented record of taking scatterings meant to destroy and making them the means of fruit. The seed only spread because the wind drove it off the floor. If you are mid-scattering now, blown somewhere you never chose, it is worth holding the possibility that you are being sown rather than discarded.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect is not always a break you make; sometimes it is one inflicted on you, forced and violent and entirely unwanted. The phase includes the scattering you would never have chosen, the rupture imposed from outside. It asks you to trust that the God who did not author the cruelty can still author the outcome, and to wonder whether you are being sown.
upheaval.inYou: The break you did not choose is not outside God's reach, and it is not outside His habit. The job lost, the relationships fractured, the displacement forced on you by someone else's cruelty, all of it can feel like wind tearing through a life that was finally settled. And settled is often exactly the problem. This does not make the cruelty good; it was evil, and God need not be thanked for the wrong to be trusted with the outcome. But He has a long record of taking scatterings meant to destroy and making them the means of fruit. The seed only spread because the wind drove it off the floor. If you are mid-scattering now, blown somewhere you never chose, you may be sown rather than discarded.
upheaval.inTheBody: Persecution and forced dispersion have, again and again, spread the Church rather than ended it. The first great scattering emptied Jerusalem and seeded Judea and Samaria; every later attempt to stamp Christianity out by driving it from its centers has tended to plant it somewhere new. The dispersions meant as catastrophe have carried the gospel into regions the Body never planned to reach. This does not bless the cruelty; God did not author the evil, though He has proven able to author the harvest. The Church driven into strange and unwanted places is not a defeated Church; it may be in its most fruitful season. The LORD plants by scattering, and the wind that thought it was dispersing chaff has been sowing the living seed of the word.
upheaval.whatRemains: When the community is scattered and the center emptied, the gospel it carries cannot be shaken. The word that the scattered went preaching does not depend on a settled address or a safe gathering. What cannot be shaken is the seed itself, the living word of God, fruitful wherever the wind carries it.
reflection: Where have I been blown by a break I did not choose, and assumed I was being discarded?
Have I been so settled and comfortable that only a scattering could move me toward what God intended?
Can I trust the God who did not author the cruelty to still author the fruit of it?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have been scattered by a break I never chose, and it has felt like being thrown away. Help me trust that You did not send the cruelty but can still sow me through it. Carry Your word wherever You have driven me, and make this scattering a planting. Amen.

notes.primary: Acts 8:1, 4 (persecution scatters the church; the scattered preach the word).

title: Receive my spirit
moment: Stephen's is the ultimate disconnect, life itself ended under a hail of stones, and the way he makes it sets the whole Christian posture toward the break. He has just preached the sermon that condemns him, and as the council grinds its teeth he looks up and sees heaven opened and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. That is too much for them. They cover their ears, rush him, drag him out of the city, and the stones begin to fall. And in the last moments of his life, two sentences come out of him, and both of them are toward someone else. First, upward: Lord Jesus, receive my spirit. He commits the one thing he still has, his own breath, into the hands of the very Lord he saw standing. Then, downward, on his knees under the stones: Lord, do not hold this sin against them. He forgives his killers in almost the same words his Lord used from the cross, and then, Luke says, he falls asleep. The first martyr shows that even the final rupture can be entered in trust and in mercy. And his blood is already seed, because a young man named Saul is standing right there, keeping the coats, watching.
voiceQuote: They stoned Stephen as he called on the Lord, saying, Lord Jesus, receive my Spirit.
scriptureText: He kneeled down, and cried with a loud voice, Lord, don't hold this sin against them. When he had said this, he fell asleep.
weight: The breaks you face in this life are not your last, and even the last one, the breaking of the body itself, can be made the way Stephen made it. Look at what his two sentences reveal. A man whose grip has already loosened. He is not clutching at his life, he hands it over; he is not clutching at his grievance, he lets it go. To entrust your spirit while it is being torn from you, and to forgive while you are still being wounded, is only possible for someone who has stopped defending himself, who fears the break less than he trusts the One receiving him. That is the whole posture of this phase distilled into a deathbed. A grip that can forgive in the middle of being broken has already let go of the fear of breaking. You are not asked to manufacture serenity or to pretend the stones do not hurt. You are invited, in every smaller rupture now and in the final one later, to fall the way Stephen fell, upward, into hands you trust, with mercy still on your lips.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect reaches its furthest edge here, in death itself, the ultimate break entered not in terror but in trust and in forgiveness. The phase asks the deepest thing it can ask: a grip loosened all the way, hands open to release both your life and your grievance. It shows that even the final rupture can be made in mercy, by someone who fears the break less than he trusts God.
upheaval.inYou: The breaks you face in this life are not your last, and even the last one, the breaking of the body itself, can be made the way Stephen made it. He does not clutch at his life, he hands it over; he does not clutch at his grievance, he lets it go. To entrust your spirit while it is torn from you, and to forgive while you are still being wounded, is only possible for someone who fears the break less than he trusts the One receiving him. You are not asked to manufacture serenity or pretend the stones do not hurt, but to fall the way Stephen fell, in every rupture now and in the final one later: upward, into hands you trust, with mercy on your lips.
upheaval.inTheBody: The Church was seeded by its martyrs, who made the ultimate break in trust and forgiveness rather than bitterness, and the whole Body still lives off what they planted. Stephen's death was not Christianity's defeat but its sowing, and the very man guarding the killers' coats became the Church's greatest apostle. So it has gone across the centuries, before a watching world: the Body's deepest losses have a way of becoming its seed, and the watchers at the edge of its suffering are often the next to be saved. The Church that loosens its grip even on its own life, refusing bitterness toward those who wound it, follows the posture of its first martyr, and finds that what looks like its end is, repeatedly, the beginning of its spread.
upheaval.whatRemains: When the body itself is broken and the breath is stoned out of a saint, what cannot be shaken is the One who receives the spirit. Stephen saw Him, standing. The hands Stephen fell into hold firm through the final rupture, and the kingdom he entered cannot be moved, even when everything else is taken.
reflection: What am I still clutching, my life or my grievance, that Stephen shows me how to release?
Do I fear the breaks ahead of me more than I trust the One who would receive me through them?
Could I forgive while I was still being wounded, or does my grip tighten the moment I am hurt?
upheaval.prayer: Lord Jesus, Stephen fell asleep entrusting You his spirit and forgiving the ones who stoned him. Loosen my grip on my life and on my grievances. When the breaks come, even the last, let me fall upward into Your hands, with mercy still on my lips, unafraid because You are standing there. Amen.

notes.primary: Acts 7:59-60 (Stephen's death; Lord, receive my spirit; do not hold this sin against them).

title: We must obey God
moment: They have already been arrested once, warned, and let go. Now they are back in the temple courts, teaching the very name they were ordered to bury, and the council has had enough. The high priest reminds them of the ban: you were strictly charged not to teach in this name, and look, you have filled Jerusalem with it. The room is heavy with the power to flog and imprison and worse, and everyone in it knows the apostles know. And Peter, who not long ago denied he had ever met the man, stands and says the thing that will be said again in every century after this one: we must obey God rather than men. It is not bravado. It is a settled order of allegiance, named out loud for the first time by the infant church. There is a God whose claim sits above the council's, and when the two collide, the higher claim wins, whatever it costs. They do not riot. They do not seize power. They simply will not be silenced about what they have seen, because the one who can punish them is not the one they ultimately answer to. On its first collision with worldly authority, the church chose God.
voiceQuote: We must obey God rather than men.
scriptureText: We are his witnesses of these things; and so also is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him.
weight: There may come a day when the people or the institution you have deferred to all your life asks of you the one thing you cannot give — to do what God forbids, or to fall silent about what He commands. The pull to comply is enormous, because deference is a habit and disapproval is a real wound and the cost of refusing is rarely small. But underneath the deference is a deeper allegiance, and an upheaval has a way of dragging it into the light. This is not a license to defy every authority you dislike; the apostles were not contrarians, and they did not break for sport. They broke at the exact point where obeying men would have meant disobeying God, and not one inch before. The line is narrow and lonely and very old. But when you finally reach it, the break of conscience is not rebellion. It is the oldest faithfulness there is — the refusal to let any earthly power take the place that belongs to God alone. The apostles drew that line on the church's first day; you stand in long company when you draw it on yours.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect here is the break of allegiance — the moment a higher claim refuses to be silenced by a lower one. The phase asks you to name, before God, who you ultimately answer to, and to hold that order even when the power that can punish you stands directly in front of you demanding otherwise.
upheaval.inYou: There may come a day when the people or the institution you have deferred to all your life asks of you the one thing you cannot give, to do what God forbids, or to fall silent about what He commands. The pull to comply is enormous, because deference is a habit and disapproval is a real wound. But underneath the deference is a deeper allegiance, and an upheaval has a way of dragging it into the light. This is no license to defy every authority you dislike; draw the line only where obeying men would mean disobeying God, not one inch before. That line is narrow and lonely and very old. But when you reach it, the break of conscience is not rebellion. It is the oldest faithfulness there is.
upheaval.inTheBody: The whole Church is finally tested on one question: whether its ultimate allegiance is to God, or to the powers that can punish it. The apostles drew that line on the Body's very first collision with worldly authority, and the Church has had to draw it again in every century since, before emperors, states, and ideologies demanding the place that belongs to God alone. Christianity that will not, when truly forced, obey God rather than men has already surrendered something it cannot get back, however many privileges it keeps. The Body is not called to defiance for its own sake; the apostles were no contrarians. But sometimes the most faithful act the Church performs before a watching world is the costly refusal to be silenced, naming whose throne is higher.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the throne above every throne. Councils and powers can charge and flog and forbid; they cannot unseat the God they presume to overrule. When the lower authority falls away, the higher one remains, and the allegiance staked on it was never misplaced.
reflection: Where am I being asked to do what God forbids, or to keep silent about what He commands?
Whom have I deferred to so long that I have let their claim creep above God's in my heart?
Am I refusing for the sake of conscience, or merely because I dislike the authority over me?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, You sit above every power that can frighten me. When obeying others would mean disobeying You, give me the apostles' settled courage to choose You. Keep me from defiance for its own sake, and steady me at the line where I must not move. Amen.

notes.primary: Acts 5:29, 32 (we must obey God rather than men).

title: Faithful unto death
moment: The proconsul does not want to kill the old man. He presses him, almost gently: just swear by the emperor, just curse the Christ, and you can go home. Polycarp is the bishop of Smyrna, very old now, and the crowd in the arena is howling for him. He has every earthly reason to say the words and live. Instead he answers that he has served Christ eighty-six years, and in all that time his King has never once wronged him; how then could he now blaspheme the one who saved him. So they burn him. The age of the martyrs is full of such hours — believers handed the simplest exit, a few words, a pinch of incense, and choosing the fire instead. The break they made was the ultimate one: not a comfort surrendered or a reputation lost, but life itself, handed over as witness. And the strange harvest of those deaths was not the church's collapse but its spread. Tertullian, looking back, would put the paradox into a single image the centuries never forgot: that the blood of the martyrs became the seed of the church. What the empire meant to stamp out, it was unknowingly sowing.
voiceQuote: Don't be afraid of the things which you are about to suffer... Be faithful to death, and I will give you the crown of life.
voiceAttribution: The risen Christ, to Smyrna — Revelation 2:10 (WEB)
scriptureText: They overcame him because of the Lamb's blood, and because of the word of their testimony. They didn't love their life, even to death.
weight: Almost none of us will be asked for our blood. But all of us, if we follow far enough, will be asked for smaller deaths — to a reputation we would rather keep, a comfort we have grown to need, a security we arranged so carefully. And the instinct is always what the proconsul offers: surely there is a few-word exit that lets you keep both Christ and the thing you are protecting. The martyrs stand against that bargain with their whole bodies. They show that the break which costs everything is not the failure of witness but its sharpest, most fruitful form — that something in the Kingdom grows precisely through what is laid down, and grows nowhere else. This is hard to believe while you stand at the cost, because surrender feels like waste and loss feels like the end. It is not the end. The seed the world tramples is the seed God is planting. Whatever in you is being asked to die for the sake of Christ, the martyrs have proven where that road leads: down into the ground first, and then up, deeper-rooted than safety could ever have made it.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect reaches its furthest edge here, where the break is life itself made into witness. The phase asks you to see that what is laid down for Christ is not lost but sown — that the costliest surrender is not the end of your testimony but its sharpest point, the seed from which more grows than any self-protection could.
upheaval.inYou: Almost none of us will be asked for our blood. But all of us, if we follow far enough, will be asked for smaller deaths, to a reputation we would keep, a comfort we have come to need, a security we arranged so carefully. The instinct is always what the proconsul offers: surely there is a few-word exit that lets you keep both Christ and the thing you are protecting. The martyrs stand against that bargain with their whole bodies. They show that the break which costs everything is not the failure of witness but its sharpest, most fruitful form, that something in the Kingdom grows through what is laid down and grows nowhere else. What you lay down for Christ goes into the ground first, and then up.
upheaval.inTheBody: Over and over, the Church has grown most exactly where it bled. The age of the martyrs did not extinguish Christianity; the empire that meant to stamp it out was unknowingly sowing it, until an ancient observer named the paradox the centuries never forgot, that the blood of the martyrs becomes the seed of the Church. Whenever the Body has been offered the simple exit, a pinch of incense, a softened word, a compromise with the powers, the faithfulness that chose the fire instead proved more fruitful. The Church tempted to preserve itself at the price of its witness should recall that its deepest roots were watered by those who would not save their lives. The seed is hidden in the dying, never in the self-protection that keeps everything barren.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the life that death cannot touch. The fire took the bishop and could not take his crown; the empire spilled the blood and only spread the faith. When everything that can be burned is burned away, the risen Christ and the life He gives remain, unconsumed.
reflection: What small death is being asked of me for the sake of Christ, and am I bargaining for an exit?
Where am I protecting a comfort or reputation more fiercely than I am following the Lord?
Can I believe that what I lay down for Him is being sown, not simply lost?
upheaval.prayer: Lord Jesus, You have never wronged me, and You gave Yourself for me first. Where You ask me to lay something down — a comfort, a name, a safety I cling to — give me the martyrs' steadiness to let it fall as witness, trusting it is seed and not waste. Amen.

notes.primary: Revelation 2:10 (be faithful unto death); Revelation 12:11 (they loved not their lives to death).
notes.tradition: References the martyrdom of Polycarp of Smyrna (c. 155 AD) and Tertullian's observation that the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church (Apologeticus, c. 197 AD); both public domain, paraphrased.

title: Do not love the world
moment: A young man in Egypt walks into church and hears the gospel read aloud as if it were addressed straight to him: go, sell what you have, and follow. Antony does not soften it into metaphor. He gives away the land he inherited, settles his sister, and walks out past the edge of the village into the desert to seek God with nothing in his hands. Others had renounced things before him; he goes further, deeper, longer, until the wilderness itself becomes his school, and in time he is reckoned the father of monasticism. What drove him out was not contempt for the world's troubles but a clear-eyed fear of its grip. He had watched a comfortable, half-compromised Christianity learn to serve God and Mammon at once, keeping its possessions and its faith in an easy truce, and he no longer believed the truce was real. No one, he had heard, can serve two masters. So he went where the second master could not follow — where there was no inheritance to guard, no comfort to protect, no rival claim whispering at his elbow. The desert was not an escape from life. It was a place stripped bare enough that a man could finally serve one Master alone.
voiceQuote: Don't love the world, neither the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the Father's love isn't in him.
scriptureText: No one can serve two masters... you can't serve both God and Mammon.
weight: Some of the world's loves are wound so tightly around your heart that they will never loosen by good intentions. You mean to hold them loosely; you tell yourself they do not own you; and meanwhile they tighten in the dark, year by year, until you cannot feel where they end and you begin. Antony's answer was a deliberate withdrawal, a chosen and costly break with the very things the world uses to own a person. Most of us are not called to literal sand and solitude, and the desert need not be a place at all. But the move Antony made is universal, and it cannot be skipped: stepping back, on purpose, from what has its hooks in you, so that your heart has room again for God. The point was never the harshness; it was the freedom on the other side of the harshness. You cannot serve two masters, and you cannot quietly negotiate with the one you mean to leave. At some point the grip only loosens when you walk, on purpose, to where it cannot reach you.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect here is the deliberate withdrawal — the chosen step back that breaks the world's grip so the heart can serve one Master. The phase asks you to stop negotiating with what owns you and to put real distance between yourself and it, trusting that the freedom waiting beyond the cost is worth the bareness it requires.
upheaval.inYou: Some loves of the world are wound too tightly around you to loosen by good intentions alone. You mean to hold them lightly; you tell yourself they do not own you; and quietly, year by year, they tighten in the dark until you can no longer feel where they end and you begin. The desert need not be a literal place, but the break Antony made is yours to make: stepping back, on purpose, from the very things the world uses to own a person, so that your heart has room again for God. You cannot serve two masters, and you cannot endlessly negotiate with the one you mean to leave. The grip rarely loosens until you walk, deliberately, to where it cannot reach you.
upheaval.inTheBody: Whenever the Church grows comfortable and entangled with wealth and power, learning to serve God and Mammon in an easy truce, the Spirit raises up movements of deliberate withdrawal that recover what the settled Church had quietly forgotten. The monastic exodus into the deserts of Egypt and beyond preserved the faith through long centuries when the institution itself had gone soft, and it has happened again and again across history, in every age the Body let the world set its terms. For the whole Church as for the soul, renewal sometimes begins not with a new program but with someone walking away from the comfortable bargain, out where the second master cannot follow.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the one Master worth the whole withdrawal. Possessions, comforts, the world's tightening grip — all of it can be left behind in the bareness; the God a stripped heart goes out to find cannot be lost. When everything the world offered falls away, He remains, and He is enough.
reflection: What love of the world has wound itself so tightly around me that good intentions no longer loosen it?
Where do I keep negotiating with something I know I am called to leave?
What deliberate step back would make room in my heart for God again?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I cannot serve two masters, and I have been trying. Show me what has its grip on me, and give me the resolve to step back on purpose, into whatever bareness it costs, until my heart has room for You alone. You are the Master worth the leaving. Amen.

notes.primary: 1 John 2:15 (do not love the world); Matthew 6:24 (you cannot serve God and Mammon).
notes.tradition: References Antony of Egypt (c. 251–356) and the birth of monasticism; public domain, paraphrased.

title: Prefer nothing to Christ
moment: The Roman world is coming apart. The old order everyone assumed was permanent is sliding into chaos, and Rome itself has become, to a young man named Benedict, a city too dissolute to live in. He does not stay to fight for it or to mourn it. He turns his back and withdraws, first to a cave and then to a community he gathers and orders by a rule of his own writing — a life balanced between prayer and work, plain and steady, governed by a single conviction he sets at its heart: that one should prefer nothing whatever to Christ. It looks, from the outside, like retreat. A man fleeing a sinking world to tend his own small garden of devotion. But the monasteries that grew from his rule became something the collapsing empire could not have imagined: arks. Through centuries of breakdown they carried Scripture, learning, and the slow disciplines of the faith, copied and prayed and kept alive when almost everything else was being lost. Benedict's break from a dying world was not an abandonment of it. It was the quiet laying of a foundation. The empire would fall. The thing he built on its margins would outlast it by a thousand years.
voiceQuote: Seek first God's Kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things will be added to you.
scriptureText: One thing is needed; Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.
weight: When the world around you is breaking apart, the instinct is to grab for control — to fight harder, manage more, hold the collapsing thing together by sheer effort. Benedict shows another move entirely, and it is easy to mistake for surrender. Sometimes the faithful response is not to seize the wheel but to withdraw and build something small, ordered, and centered on Christ, while the larger order does whatever it is going to do. This is not passivity, and it is not despair. It is the recognition that you cannot save the empire, but you can, by grace, build an ark. The work looks modest from the outside — a rule, a rhythm, a handful of committed people, nothing that will make headlines while the headlines are full of collapse. But the modest, ordered, Christ-centered thing has a way of outlasting the spectacular thing that scorned it. The foundation you lay quietly now, in a season when everyone else is scrambling, may be the floor that others stand on long after the crisis that frightened you has passed into history. Prefer nothing to Christ, and build.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect here looks like retreat but is actually foundation-laying. The phase asks you to resist the urge to grab for control of a collapsing order and instead to withdraw and build something small, steady, and centered on Christ — trusting that the modest thing you raise on the margins may outlast everything that is presently falling.
upheaval.inYou: When the world around you is coming apart, the instinct is to grab for control, to fight harder and manage more and hold the collapsing thing together by sheer effort. The faithful move may be the opposite, and it can look like surrender: to withdraw and build something small, ordered, and centered on Christ, while the larger order does whatever it is going to do. This is not passivity or despair. It is the recognition that you cannot save the empire, but you can, by grace, build an ark. Benedict shows the break that looks like mere retreat and is actually the laying of a foundation. Build your ark quietly now; others may stand on it long after the crisis that frightened you has passed.
upheaval.inTheBody: In the Church's most chaotic eras, renewal has often come not from the threatened center but from those who quietly disconnected to build something stable and Christ-centered on the margins. As the Roman world slid into ruin, the monastery outlasted the empire, carrying Scripture, learning, and the slow disciplines of the faith through centuries of breakdown when almost everything else was lost. The pattern recurs across the whole Body: when the permanent-seeming Christian order collapses, the faith is kept not by those scrambling to hold the spectacular thing together but by small, ordered communities of the deeply committed who prefer nothing whatever to Christ. They have carried the Church through collapse before, and can carry it again.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the Christ to whom nothing is to be preferred. Empires crumble and the permanent-seeming order slides into chaos, but the One the ark was built around does not slide with it. When everything assumed to be lasting has fallen, He remains, and what was built on Him remains with Him.
reflection: Where am I grabbing for control of something collapsing, when I am called instead to withdraw and build?
What small, ordered, Christ-centered thing could I lay as a foundation in this unsteady season?
Is there anything I am presently preferring to Christ that the shaking is asking me to set beneath Him?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, when the world I trusted is coming apart, keep me from grabbing wildly for control. Teach me to withdraw and build something small and steady around You, preferring nothing whatever to You. Let me lay a quiet foundation others can stand on, long after the collapse has passed. Amen.

notes.primary: Matthew 6:33 (seek first the Kingdom); Luke 10:42 (one thing is needful).
notes.tradition: References Benedict of Nursia (c. 480–547), his Rule, and Benedictine monasticism preserving learning and faith through the fall of Rome; the maxim to prefer nothing whatever to Christ is paraphrased from the Rule.

title: No enduring city here
moment: In 410 the unthinkable happens. Rome, the eternal city, the order beneath everyone's feet for as long as anyone could remember, is sacked. And among Christians the panic runs deeper than the grief, because by now the empire is Christian, and its fall raises a terrible question: is God's own cause finished, now that the Christian empire has fallen with it. Into that fear Augustine writes, slowly, across years, the great work that answers it: the City of God. There are two cities, he says, woven together through all history — one earthly, built on love of self, and one eternal, built on love of God — and the church's hope was never the earthly city, glorious as it had seemed and easy as it had been to confuse with the Kingdom. Its true home is the city to come, the one whose builder and maker is God. So the fall of Rome, for all its horror, was not the end of the faith. It was the first of the great upheavals that, as Phyllis Tickle would much later observe, seem to shake the church roughly every five hundred years — cracking open whatever cultural shell it has hardened into. The empire fell, and the church was forced to tear its hope loose from a perishing order.
voiceQuote: We don't have here an enduring city, but we seek that which is to come.
voiceAttribution: The letter to the Hebrews — Hebrews 13:14 (WEB)
scriptureText: He looked for the city which has the foundations, whose builder and maker is God.
weight: When an order you assumed was permanent collapses — a career, an institution, a marriage, a whole world you trusted to hold — the disconnect is brutal, and the first thing it threatens is your sense that anything is solid at all. If that could fall, you think, then nothing is safe. But Augustine's word still stands across sixteen centuries: we have no enduring city here. The thing that fell was never your foundation, however much you had let it feel like one. You had simply confused a particular order, a familiar arrangement, with the Kingdom itself — the way the Christians of 410 confused Rome with the cause of God. The shaking is terrible, but it is also clarifying. It pries your hope loose from what could never finally bear its weight and frees it to rest where it actually belongs: on the city to come, the one whose builder is God, the one no sack can reach. What fell was a city of man. Your true home was never in the rubble. It is still being built, and its maker does not fail.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect here is the collapse that tears hope loose from a perishing order — the first of the great roughly-five-hundred-year upheavals of the Church, and a pattern that reaches every shaken life. The phase asks you to grieve what fell while refusing to call it your foundation, and to let the shaking relocate your hope onto the city that cannot fall.
upheaval.inYou: When an order you assumed was permanent collapses, a career, an institution, a marriage, a whole world you trusted to hold, the disconnect is brutal, and the first thing it threatens is your sense that anything is solid at all. If that could fall, you think, then nothing is safe. But the old word still holds across the centuries: you have no enduring city here. What fell was never your foundation, however much you had let it feel like one. You had simply confused a familiar arrangement with the Kingdom itself. The shaking is frightening, and it is also clarifying. It pries your hope loose from what could never finally bear its weight, and frees it to rest where it actually belongs, on the city to come.
upheaval.inTheBody: The Church repeatedly mistakes a particular cultural order for the Kingdom itself, and is repeatedly shaken when that order falls. When Rome was sacked in 410 the panic among Christians ran deeper than the grief, for the empire was Christian by then, and its fall raised the terrible question of whether God's own cause was finished. Augustine answered that the Church's home was never the earthly city, glorious as it had seemed, but the city to come, whose builder and maker is God. This is the first of the great upheavals that, as Phyllis Tickle later observed, seem to shake the Church roughly every five hundred years, cracking open whatever cultural shell it has hardened into and tearing its hope loose from a perishing world before a watching age.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the city whose builder and maker is God. Empires are sacked and permanent-seeming orders perish; the city to come is not built by hands that can fail, and no fall can reach it. When the city of man lies in rubble, the city of God still stands, still rising, still sure.
reflection: What order in my life did I quietly mistake for my foundation, only to feel it shake?
Where have I confused a familiar arrangement with the Kingdom of God itself?
Can I let this collapse relocate my hope onto the city that cannot fall?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, an order I trusted as permanent has shaken, and I felt as if nothing were solid. Remind me I have no enduring city here. Tear my hope loose from what could never hold it, and fasten it on the city to come, whose builder and maker is You. That city cannot fall. Amen.

notes.primary: Hebrews 13:14 (no enduring city; we seek the one to come); Hebrews 11:10 (the city whose builder is God).
notes.tradition: References Augustine's City of God (c. 413–426, public domain, paraphrased) and the sack of Rome (410); resonant with Phyllis Tickle's roughly-500-year pattern of upheaval (The Great Emergence, 2008), paraphrased and attributed.

title: That they may be one
moment: In 1054, after centuries of slow drift in language, custom, and the question of who finally speaks for the church, the breach goes formal. Papal legates from the Latin West stride into Hagia Sophia in the Greek East and lay a parchment of excommunication on the altar itself, in the middle of the liturgy. The patriarch of Constantinople answers in kind. With that exchange the one church of Christ cracks down the seam between East and West, and the crack does not close. A thousand years later it is still open. We are tempted to read every great break in these pages as a holy one, a brave disconnect from what had gone wrong. This one will not let us. There is no recovered gospel here, no truth set loose, no lamp handed to the people. There is only a body tearing, pride answering pride, two halves of the church declaring the other cut off. It is the hard truth the whole phase has to hold: not every break is obedience. Some are simply wounds. And this wound was laid across the very prayer Jesus prayed in the upper room, that they all might be one.
voiceQuote: That they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you... that the world may believe that you sent me.
voiceAttribution: Jesus, praying for his church — John 17:21 (WEB)
scriptureText: Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized into the name of Paul?
weight: We need this day precisely because the others can intoxicate us. Read enough stories of holy disconnect and a person starts to think every rupture they cause is courage, every relationship they sever a stand for truth, every community they walk out on a corrupt thing they were right to leave. The Great Schism is here to sober us. Some of your breaks are righteous, and some are just the old pride dressed up as conviction. Severance by stubbornness. Walls built because apologizing felt like losing. A friendship, a marriage, a congregation torn not because God asked it but because neither side would yield first.
