Disconnect is the first phase of renewal, yes, but it has a counterfeit, and the counterfeit looks almost identical from the inside. The difference is not in how justified you feel. The difference is what the break serves. So when a relationship lies in pieces, do not reach automatically for the language of brave obedience. Ask whether this is a break to honor or a tearing to grieve and, if you can, to mend. Some disconnects call for celebration. This kind calls for repentance.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect, in its sobering form. The phase that ignites renewal has a shadow, and this is it: the break that is not obedience but injury. Here the phase asks for honesty rather than nerve. It asks you to tell the necessary break from the avoidable one, and to grieve the tearing of Christ's body instead of boasting in it.
upheaval.inYou: Be honest about your own ruptures. Read enough stories of brave disconnect and you start to think every rupture you cause is courage, every relationship you sever a stand for truth. Some of your breaks are righteous; some are the old pride dressed up as conviction: severance by stubbornness, walls built because apologizing felt like losing, a friendship or a marriage torn not because God asked it but because neither side would yield first. The counterfeit looks almost identical from the inside; the difference is not how justified you feel but what the break serves. Not every disconnect you have made was obedience. Some are waiting, even now, not for a defense but for repentance you have been too proud to attempt.
upheaval.inTheBody: Not all the Church's divisions are glorious reformations; many are only schisms, wounds that contradict the very oneness Christ asked of the Father in the upper room. In 1054 the one Church of Christ cracked down the seam between East and West, papal legates laying excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia and the patriarch answering in kind, and a thousand years later the crack has not closed. There was no recovered gospel there, no truth set loose, only a body tearing and pride answering pride. The whole Church must learn to tell the break it cannot avoid from the split it merely refuses to heal. The Body of Christ torn is never a trophy. It is a grief, and it ought to be carried like one before a watching world.
upheaval.whatRemains: Beneath every tearing, the church Christ prayed for is still one in Him, however divided it stands in time. What cannot be shaken is His own prayer, that they all may be one, already answered at the root even where it waits, century after century, to be answered on the surface.
reflection: Which of my broken relationships did I sever for conviction, and which for pride I dressed up as conviction?
Where have I called a break holy obedience when honesty would name it an avoidable wound?
Is there a tearing in my life that God is asking me to grieve, and perhaps to begin repairing, rather than defend?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, You prayed that we would be one, and I have torn what You meant to hold together. Teach me to tell the break I must make from the one I should never have made. Where I have severed in pride, give me the courage to grieve it and the humility to mend it. Amen.

notes.primary: John 17:21 (that they may all be one); 1 Corinthians 1:13 (is Christ divided?).
notes.tradition: References the Great Schism of 1054 between the Eastern and Western church; resonant with Phyllis Tickle's roughly-500-year pattern of upheaval (The Great Emergence, 2008), paraphrased and attributed.

title: Take no gold
moment: Francis is the son of a wealthy cloth merchant in Assisi, raised to inherit a fortune in fine fabric and the comfortable Christianity that came folded in with it. Then the gospel's plain command to the twelve reaches him without padding: carry no gold, no silver, no money in your belt. He takes it literally, all the way to the skin. In the public square, before the bishop and a gathering crowd and his furious father, Francis strips off the costly clothes that mark him as his father's heir, hands them back, and stands there with nothing. He walks out of that square wedded to what he will call Lady Poverty, owning nothing, begging his bread, repairing broken chapels with his own hands. It looks like madness, a rich boy throwing his birthright into the dirt. It is the spark of a renewal that will sweep through the whole medieval church. He does not argue the comfortable Christians out of their comfort. He simply lives the gospel's instruction so nakedly, so completely, that the contrast itself becomes the sermon. He took no gold, and the church remembered, watching him, what it had quietly let itself forget.
voiceQuote: Don't take any gold, nor silver, nor brass in your money belts.
scriptureText: You know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that you through his poverty might become rich.
weight: The grip of money does not loosen because you decide it should. It loosens through breaks, and usually only through breaks that cost. Francis is the extreme edge of this, and you are almost certainly not called as far as the public square and the bare skin and the begging bowl. But the principle underneath his extremity reaches every one of us. Real freedom from Mammon is rarely a change of heart you merely intend. It tends to require an actual act of release, a hand opened and something genuinely let go, money given where it leaves a mark. You can feel generous for years while your grip never actually loosens, because the feeling costs nothing and the grip was never tested. Francis tested his all the way to the bone. The question his break leaves is not whether you admire him; almost everyone admires him from a safe distance. The question is whether there is one concrete, costing release you have been intending and never making. Lady Poverty does not marry the well-meaning. She marries those who actually walk out of the square.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect, made costly and visible. This is the deliberate break with wealth that sparks renewal where comfort had dulled it. The phase asks for more than a softened heart toward money; it asks for the act itself, the concrete release. Disconnect here means an open hand that actually opens, and a hold on security you actually let fall.
upheaval.inYou: The grip money has on you does not loosen because you decide it should. It loosens through breaks, and usually only through breaks that cost. Francis stands at the extreme edge of this, and you are almost certainly not called as far as the bare skin and the begging bowl. But the principle beneath his extremity reaches you. Real freedom from Mammon is rarely a change of heart you merely intend; it tends to require an actual release, a hand opened and something genuinely let go, money given where it leaves a mark. You can feel generous for years while your grip never truly loosens, because the feeling costs nothing and the grip was never tested. The question is whether there is one concrete, costing release you have been intending and never making.
upheaval.inTheBody: When the Church grows rich and the gospel grows comfortable, renewal has repeatedly come through movements of radical simplicity, the friars and reformers and the voluntarily poor who broke with wealth and shamed the comfortable Church back toward Christ. Francis stripping off his costly clothes in the square at Assisi did not argue the prosperous out of their prosperity; he simply lived the gospel's plain command so nakedly that the contrast itself became the sermon, and the medieval Church remembered, watching him, what it had quietly let itself forget. The visible break with Mammon carries a strange renewing power across the whole Body. A people that has forgotten the gospel remembers it, watching someone live it all the way to the skin before a watching world.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the Christ who, being rich, became poor for our sakes, that we through His poverty might become rich. Every fortune surrendered points to His. The wealth Mammon offers is shaken and falls; the riches that come through His chosen poverty cannot be taken away.
reflection: Where is my generosity an intention I admire in myself but have never actually acted on?
What concrete, costing release have I been putting off because letting go would leave a real mark?
What does my grip on money tell me about who I am quietly serving?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, You who were rich became poor so that I might be rich in You, and still my hands close tight around what I have. Loosen them. Show me the one release I have only ever intended, and give me courage to make it. Free me from Mammon, all the way to the bone. Amen.

notes.primary: Matthew 10:9 (take no gold); 2 Corinthians 8:9 (though rich, he became poor).
notes.tradition: References Francis of Assisi (c. 1181–1226) and his renunciation of wealth; public domain, paraphrased.

title: A lamp to my feet
moment: John Wycliffe is an Oxford scholar with a dangerous conviction: that the plain people of England have a right to read the Scriptures in the tongue they actually speak. In his day the Bible is kept in Latin, locked inside the learning of the few, and the few have no intention of handing over the key. Wycliffe sets about translating it into English anyway, against fierce and powerful opposition, and his followers carry the hand-copied pages out across the country. He is the morning star of the Reformation, glimmering more than a century before Luther is born. His break is not against the faith but against a stranglehold on it: he means to take the Word out of the exclusive keeping of the gatekeepers and put the lamp directly into the hands of the people whose feet it was given to light. The establishment condemns him. But the deepest measure of how much his break frightened them comes after he is already dead and buried: decades later they dig up his bones, burn them to ash, and scatter the ash in a river, as if a man could be unsaid by destroying his corpse. The pages were already loose. You cannot burn a thing the people now carry for themselves.
voiceQuote: Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.
scriptureText: The word is very near to you, in your mouth, and in your heart, that you may do it.
weight: Sometimes the faithful break is the simple, stubborn insistence that what has been locked away belongs to everyone. The light was never meant to fall only on the path of the credentialed; it was given for the feet of ordinary people, the unlearned, the ones the gatekeepers assume cannot be trusted with it. There is a quiet violence in hoarding access to God, in standing between people and the Word as though you were the custodian of a private treasure rather than a servant handing out bread. Wycliffe's disconnect from the establishment was, underneath all the scholarship and the controversy, exactly this refusal: he would not let the Word be kept from the people it was given to. When you sense that some good thing meant for everyone has been quietly fenced off and made the possession of a few, the faithful break may be to climb the fence and start handing it out. They can burn the man. They learned, too late, that they could not burn what he had already put into common hands. The Word, once loosed among the people, does not go back into the cabinet.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect that breaks a lock. This is the break that takes the Word out of exclusive keeping and puts it into common hands. The phase asks you to refuse the hoarding of what God meant for everyone, and to bear the establishment's wrath for it. Disconnect here means prying open access that someone has fenced, and trusting the loosed Word to outlast the fury.
upheaval.inYou: Sometimes your faithful break is the simple, stubborn insistence that what has been locked away belongs to everyone. The light was never meant to fall only on the path of the credentialed; it was given for the feet of ordinary people, the unlearned, the ones the gatekeepers assume cannot be trusted with it. There is a quiet violence in hoarding access to God, in standing between people and the Word as though you were the custodian of a private treasure rather than a servant handing out bread. When some good thing meant for everyone has been quietly fenced off as the possession of a few, the faithful break may simply be to climb the fence and start handing it out.
upheaval.inTheBody: The Church has sometimes guarded access to God as though it were the gatekeeper's private possession, locking Scripture and prayer and nearness behind a guild and assuming the plain people could not be trusted with the key. Wycliffe, the morning star of the Reformation, set about putting the Word into the tongue England actually spoke, against fierce opposition, more than a century before Luther. Renewal across the whole Body breaks such locks and puts the lamp back into the hands of all the people. They condemned him and even dug up his bones decades later to burn them to ash, but the movement his break began was already loose in the land, and ashes in a river could not stop it.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the Word itself, near to you, in your mouth and in your heart. Gatekeepers rise and fall and fences are torn down; the lamp that lights the path endures. They burned the translator to ash, and the light he carried to the people only spread.
reflection: What good thing meant for everyone have I let myself believe belongs only to the qualified few?
Where am I standing as a gatekeeper between people and something God meant to give them freely?
Is there a lock I am being asked to break, whatever the cost, so that others can reach what I have?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, Your Word is a lamp for the feet of ordinary people, not a treasure for the few to hoard. Where I have fenced off what You meant to give freely, forgive me. Make me one who hands out the bread, and let me trust the light, once loosed, to do what I cannot. Amen.

notes.primary: Psalm 119:105 (your word is a lamp); Deuteronomy 30:14 (the word is very near you).
notes.tradition: References John Wycliffe (c. 1328–1384), the Wycliffite English Bible, and his title as the morning star of the Reformation; public domain, paraphrased.

title: Do not fear those who kill the body
moment: Jan Hus, the Bohemian preacher, is summoned to the Council of Constance in 1415 under a promise of safe conduct, a guarantee that he may come and answer for his teaching and return home unharmed. The promise is broken. He is condemned and handed to the flames, a full century before Luther, for the crime of preaching reform the council would not hear. To the end they press him to recant. He will not, because no one has shown him from Scripture that what he taught was wrong, and he will not unsay the truth merely to save his skin. So he goes to the stake holding to conscience and the Word against the combined weight of the council that can burn him. Tradition remembers something he is said to have spoken near the end. His name, in his own tongue, meant goose; they were roasting the goose now, he said, but after him would come a swan they would not be able to silence. A hundred years later, watching Luther, Protestants would read those words as prophecy fulfilled. They lit the fire believing it would end him. It announced what was coming instead.
voiceQuote: Don't be afraid of those who kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul.
scriptureText: In all these things, we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.
weight: The break that will not recant under pressure is rare, and it is terribly costly. Most of us bend long before the fire; we trim the truth to keep the peace, soften what we know to spare ourselves the council's displeasure. Hus shows the disconnect carried all the way to its furthest edge, the one that prefers death to a lie, that holds to conscience and Scripture when the price for holding is everything. Few of us will ever have our convictions tested by literal flame. But the smaller versions arrive constantly: the moment when one quiet retraction would buy back your safety or your standing or your place at the table, and the only thing stopping you is that it would be untrue. The question Hus leaves is not whether you would be brave at the stake; that scene is mercifully far from most lives. It is whether your yes is still yes when keeping it costs you something real. His was. They could break his body. They could not make him say the lie, and the truth he refused to unsay outlived the men who burned him.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect that will not recant. This is the break held to the end, even at the cost of the body. The phase asks for a conscience bound to Scripture that prefers death to a lie, and a yes that stays yes when the council demands otherwise. Disconnect here means refusing to unsay the truth, and trusting that the fire which seems to end you may only announce what is coming.
upheaval.inYou: The break that will not recant under pressure, that holds to conscience and Scripture even when the cost is everything, is rare and terribly costly. Most of us bend long before any fire; we trim the truth to keep the peace, soften what we know to spare ourselves the displeasure of those who can punish us. Few of your breaks will ever be tested by literal flame. But the smaller versions arrive constantly: the moment when one quiet retraction would buy back your safety or your standing or your place at the table, and the only thing stopping you is that it would be untrue. The question is not whether you would be brave at the stake. It is whether your yes is still yes when keeping it costs you something real.
upheaval.inTheBody: The Church's reformers have often been silenced, exiled, or killed by the very institution they tried to renew, and the renewal arrived anyway, a generation on. Jan Hus was promised safe conduct to the Council of Constance in 1415, then condemned and handed to the flames a full century before Luther, because no one had shown him from Scripture that what he taught was wrong and he would not unsay the truth to save his skin. Tradition remembers his word that they were roasting the goose now, but a swan would come they could not silence. So it goes across the whole Body: the break the establishment believes it has stamped out has a way of returning as a fire that cannot be put out. What a council means to end, it sometimes only announces.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the soul they could not kill. They burned the body and lost the man, for the One who holds him is past their reach. Through the love of Christ a martyr is made more than a conqueror in the fire, and the truth a conscience refuses to unsay outlives every flame meant to silence it.
reflection: Where is my yes quietly becoming no because holding to it would cost me my safety or standing?
What truth do I know that I have been trimming to keep the peace with those who can punish me?
Can I trust that what is faithful in me will outlast the pressure that means to silence it?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I bend so easily, trimming the truth to spare myself. Bind my conscience to Your Word as You bound those who would not recant. When my yes is pressed to become a lie, hold me. They could not kill the soul You keep; let the faithful word outlive every fire. Amen.

notes.primary: Matthew 10:28 (do not fear those who kill the body); Romans 8:37 (more than conquerors).
notes.tradition: References Jan Hus (c. 1369–1415), burned at the Council of Constance, and the goose/swan tradition later associated with Luther; public domain, paraphrased; the prophecy noted as tradition.

title: Do not look back
figure: The break you cannot stay in
moment: Lot does not leave Sodom; he is dragged out of it. The angels take him by the hand because he lingers, and they put a blunt command into his ears as the city's last morning breaks: escape for your life, do not look behind you, do not stop anywhere in the plain, flee to the hills or you will be swept away. There is nothing majestic about this departure. It is not a calling like Abram's, summoned out toward a promise; it is a rescue, God prying a man loose from a place that is about to be destroyed under him. And then the sentence that has haunted readers ever since: his wife looks back. Behind her the plain is burning, and her heart is still turned toward it, still bound to what is going up in smoke, and she is lost where she stands, frozen into a pillar of salt by her own longing for the thing that was killing her. Not every disconnect in these pages is glorious vocation. Some are simply the urgent, unglamorous work of getting out before the fire reaches you, and not turning around to mourn the ruin you were rescued from.
voiceQuote: Escape for your life. Don't look behind you, neither stay anywhere in the plain. Escape to the mountain, lest you be consumed.
scriptureText: If they had been thinking of that country from which they went out, they would have had time to return. But now they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one.
weight: Some of your breaks are not a grand calling at all. They are escapes. God prying you out of an environment, a relationship, a habit that was quietly consuming you while you lingered and told yourself it was not so bad. There is no shame in a disconnect that is nothing more than survival. You do not need the departure to be noble for it to be God's mercy; sometimes the whole of His kindness in a season is simply that He got you out. But the story sets a sharp warning beside the rescue. The danger is not the fire you fled. It is the backward look, the slow turn of the heart toward the very thing that was destroying you, the nostalgia that gilds the ruin and calls it home. That look is what turns the rescued into a pillar of salt. So if your break was an escape, let it be an escape all the way through. Grieve what you have lost, if you must. But do not stand on the road out romanticizing the burning city. Escape for your life, and do not look behind you.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect as rescue, not vocation. This is not the break of a calling but the break of getting out, God prying you loose from what would have destroyed you. The phase asks only that you go, and that you keep facing forward. Disconnect here means fleeing what is consuming you and refusing the backward look that romanticizes the ruin you were saved from.
upheaval.inYou: Maybe your break is not a grand calling at all but an escape, God prying you out of an environment, a relationship, a habit that was quietly consuming you while you lingered and told yourself it was not so bad. There is no shame in a disconnect that is nothing more than survival; you do not need the departure to be noble for it to be mercy. Sometimes the whole of His kindness in a season is simply that He got you out. But the real danger is not the fire you fled. It is the backward look, the slow turn of the heart toward the thing that was destroying you, the nostalgia that gilds the ruin and calls it home. Escape for your life, and do not turn around to grieve the burning city.
upheaval.inTheBody: Sometimes the Church, or a whole tradition within it, must simply flee what has gone toxic, a system turned corrupt, an abuse that cannot be reformed from within but can only be left. The break of escape is legitimate; not every leaving by the people of God is a failure of faithfulness. Lot did not depart Sodom in triumph; the angels dragged him out by the hand because he lingered, and the command was blunt, to flee and not look behind. The peril for the whole Body is the same as for the soul: the backward look, the nostalgia for the very order that was destroying it, the slow turn of the heart that gilds the ruin. That look is what turns the rescued into a pillar of salt.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the better country ahead, the one God is bringing you toward rather than the one He pulled you from. The burning city had no foundation that could hold. Stop longing for it, and your hope is free to rest on the city that endures, whose builder and maker is God.
reflection: Is my break a calling outward, or is it a rescue I should simply accept without needing it to be noble?
Where is my heart still turned back toward something that was quietly consuming me?
What am I romanticizing about a place or pattern God may have pulled me out of for my life?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, sometimes Your mercy is simply that You got me out. Thank You for the rescue I did not earn. Keep my heart from turning back toward the fire I fled, from gilding the ruin that was destroying me. Set my face toward the country You are bringing me to. Amen.

notes.primary: Genesis 19:17 (escape for your life, do not look back); Hebrews 11:15-16 (they desire a better country).

title: The righteous shall live by faith
moment: A monk in Wittenberg cannot quiet his conscience. Martin Luther has fasted, confessed, and punished his body, and still the guilt will not lift; the more he strives to make himself righteous, the more unrighteous he feels. Then, laboring over Paul's letter to the Romans, he is stopped by a single line — that the righteous shall live by faith. The righteousness God demands is the righteousness God gives. It is received, not earned. The discovery does not merely comfort him; it breaks him clean away from an entire machinery of merit, penance, and purchased pardon he had been exhausting himself to satisfy. On the last day of October, 1517, he posts ninety-five theses against the sale of indulgences on the door of the castle church, intending only to open a scholarly debate among scholars. He gets something else. The argument escapes the academy, runs across a continent on the new printing presses, and will not be recalled. He meant a disputation. What began was the Reformation — the great Western rummage sale, arriving roughly five hundred years after the last one shook the church.
voiceQuote: Therein is revealed a righteousness of God from faith to faith. As it is written, The righteous shall live by faith.
scriptureText: By grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God.
weight: The deepest break in a life can begin with one recovered truth that quietly dismantles a whole false system you had been straining to hold up. Luther was not trying to start a revolution; he was trying to find peace. And when he found that the thing he had been killing himself to earn had been a gift the entire time, the floor of the old striving simply gave way beneath him. That is how grace often arrives — not as a gentle addition to your effort but as the end of it. Notice that he did not engineer the rupture. He pulled one thread, honestly, because his conscience would not let it alone, and the garment came apart in his hands. So it tends to go. You do not always have to plan the demolition. Sometimes you only have to stop pretending the one true thing you have seen is not true, and follow it where it leads. The disconnect from the old, exhausting bargain is not the loss it first appears. For a soul that has been earning and earning and never arriving, it is release.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect is the break, and here it is the break a single recovered truth makes in a whole false system. The phase does not ask you to manufacture rupture. It asks you to be honest about the one thing you have seen, and to follow it even when you cannot see where it will lead or how much it will cost.
upheaval.inYou: You may be holding up some elaborate structure of earning, proving, performing, paying down a debt you can never quite clear. The break begins the moment one recovered truth quietly dismantles it: that what you strained to earn was given all along. That is how grace often arrives, not as a gentle addition to your effort but as the end of it. Notice that you do not always have to engineer the rupture. You only have to stop pretending the one true thing you have seen is not true, and follow it where it leads. The disconnect from the old, exhausting bargain is not the loss it first appears. For a soul that has been earning and earning and never arriving, it is release, the first full breath you have drawn in years.
upheaval.inTheBody: Roughly every five hundred years the Church's distortions harden until something has to give, and God uses one person to name the truth that brings the rotten scaffolding down. A monk in Wittenberg, laboring over Paul's letter to the Romans, was stopped by a single line, that the righteous shall live by faith, and the discovery broke him clean away from an entire machinery of merit and purchased pardon. Luther meant only to open a scholarly debate; the argument escaped the academy, ran across a continent on the new printing presses, and would not be recalled. So the renewal that shakes the whole Body often begins far smaller, and far more accidentally, than anyone living through it intends, the great Western rummage sale arriving on schedule once again.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the grace that was always a gift and never a wage. Systems of merit rise and harden and finally fall, but the righteousness God gives does not depend on the machinery built around it. When the scaffolding comes down, what stands is the gift it had buried.
reflection: What structure of earning am I exhausting myself to hold up right now?
Is there one true thing I have seen that I keep refusing to follow because of where it might lead?
Can I believe that what I have been straining to earn was meant to be received?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have worn myself out trying to earn what You meant to give. Break me free of the old bargain. Let me receive the grace I cannot purchase, and follow the truth You have shown me even when I cannot see the end of it. Amen.

notes.primary: Romans 1:17 (the righteous shall live by faith); Ephesians 2:8 (by grace, through faith).
notes.tradition: References Martin Luther (1483–1546), the ninety-five theses (1517), and the recovery of justification by faith; resonant with Phyllis Tickle's roughly-500-year pattern of upheaval (The Great Emergence, 2008), paraphrased and attributed.

title: We cannot but speak
moment: Four years after the theses, the monk stands in a hall at Worms before the Emperor himself, his books piled on a table, and is ordered to take it all back. He does not answer at once. He asks for a night, and is given it. When he returns the next day the room is waiting for a single word, recant, and he will not say it. Unless he is convinced by Scripture and plain reason, he tells them, his conscience is bound — held captive — to the Word of God, and to act against conscience is neither safe nor right. Tradition hands down the ringing close, that here he stands and can do no other; whether those exact words were his or were set down later, the substance was unmistakable. One man, with no army and no protector he could trust, against the assembled weight of empire and church, declined to unsay what he had seen. Like the apostles dragged before their own council, he found he simply could not help speaking of it. The break was now public, and it could not be taken back.
voiceQuote: We can't help telling the things which we saw and heard.
voiceAttribution: Peter and John, before the council — Acts 4:20 (WEB)
scriptureText: I will speak of your statutes before kings, and will not be put to shame.
weight: There come moments when retreat would be so much easier, and a conscience bound to the truth still cannot take it. You know the feeling, even on a smaller scale: the meeting where one honest word will cost you, and the silence that would cost you nothing but yourself. The stand is terrifying and freeing in the same breath, because the instant you make it you stop carrying the exhausting weight of the lie you were tempted to tell. Notice what Luther's stand was not. It was not stubbornness dressed up as principle, not the love of being the lone holdout. He had asked for a night; he was not eager. The break of standing is for people who would genuinely rather sit down and cannot. When the truth has taken your conscience captive, you discover that obedience and freedom are the same motion — that to betray what you have seen, even to keep the peace, would be the real imprisonment. Sometimes you cannot help speaking of what you have seen and heard, whatever it finally costs you.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect here is public and irrevocable — the moment a conscience captive to the Word makes its break in the open, where it cannot be unmade. The phase asks whether you will stand on the truth against the full weight of pressure, not for the thrill of defiance, but because betraying what you have seen has become impossible.
upheaval.inYou: There is a moment coming, or already here, when retreat would be so much easier, and a conscience bound to the truth still cannot take it. You know the feeling even on a small scale: the meeting where one honest word will cost you, and the silence that would cost you nothing but yourself. The break of standing is terrifying and freeing in the same breath, because the instant you make it you stop carrying the exhausting weight of the lie you were tempted to tell. Be sure it is not stubbornness dressed up as principle, not the love of being the lone holdout. Like the apostles before the council, you may find you simply cannot help speaking of what you have seen and heard, whatever it finally costs.
upheaval.inTheBody: The whole Church depends, at the decisive hours of its history, on those who will stand on the Word against the entire machinery of institutional pressure. Four years after his theses, Luther stood in the hall at Worms before the Emperor, his books piled on the table, ordered to take it all back, and would not, his conscience held captive to the Word of God. It was not contrarianism but a refusal to purchase peace with the truth, and tradition hands down the ringing close, that here he stands and can do no other. A Body that never produces such stands has quietly agreed that keeping the peace matters more than keeping faith. The truth the Church has actually seen does not bend to the size of the room arrayed against it.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the Word that takes a conscience captive and will not release it to a comfortable lie. Empires convene and councils threaten and the pressure to recant is immense, but the truth a person has actually seen does not bend to the size of the room arrayed against it.
reflection: Where is silence the easy road for me right now, and what would honest speech cost?
Is my conviction a conscience bound to the truth, or am I in love with being the lone holdout?
What have I seen and heard that I can no longer, in good conscience, keep quiet about?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, when retreat is easy and standing is costly, hold my conscience captive to Your Word. Keep me from both cowardice and mere stubbornness. Give me the strange freedom of those who cannot help speaking of what they have seen, whatever it costs. Amen.

notes.primary: Acts 4:20 (we cannot help telling what we saw and heard); Psalm 119:46 (I will speak before kings).
notes.tradition: References Luther at the Diet of Worms (1521); the famous wording Here I stand, I can do no other is noted as traditional and possibly a later addition to his recorded reply.

title: Light for the simple
moment: William Tyndale is gripped by one stubborn conviction: that the boy following a plow through an English field ought to know the Scriptures better than the learned clergy who have kept them locked away in Latin. He is told, in effect, that this is not for plowboys, and he answers with the vow that defines his life — that if God spares him, he will see to it that very boy knows more of the Bible than they do. Forbidden to translate in England, he flees to the continent, and there produces the first printed English New Testament. The copies come home by smuggling, hidden in bales of cloth and sacks of grain, slipping past the men who would burn them. For years he works on, hunted. At last he is betrayed, seized, and condemned; near Brussels he is strangled and his body burned, and his final breath is spent praying that God would open the eyes of England's king. The prayer was not wasted. Within a few short years an English Bible the king himself authorized stood open in every parish church in the land.
voiceQuote: The entrance of your words gives light; it gives understanding to the simple.
scriptureText: So shall my word be that goes forth out of my mouth: it shall not return to me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please.
weight: Some breaks are not for your own advancement at all but for someone else's access — giving away, at real cost, the very thing you were told to keep under lock. Tyndale gained nothing for himself by his disconnect from safety and sanction; he gained exile, poverty, and finally a martyr's death. What he won was for the plowboy, for the unlettered and the simple, for everyone the gatekeepers had decided did not need the light. There is a particular holiness in that kind of rupture — the break made on behalf of people who may never know your name. It is easy to leave a thing for your own freedom. It is a harder and rarer thing to break with the establishment so that others, not you, can have what it was hoarding. The entrance of God's words gives understanding to the simple, and Tyndale died to make that promise literally true on English soil. Notice how the Word behaves once it is loosed: it does not return empty. Burn the translator, and the translation fills the churches anyway.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect here is the break made for the sake of others' access rather than one's own advancement. The phase asks whether you are willing to give away, at cost, what you were told to keep — to lose your safety not for your own freedom but so that the locked-away light can fall on people who were never meant to be kept from it.
upheaval.inYou: Some breaks are not for your own advancement at all but for someone else's access, giving away, at real cost, the very thing you were told to keep under lock. There is a particular holiness in that kind of rupture, the break made on behalf of people who may never know your name. It is easy to leave a thing for your own freedom. It is a harder and rarer thing to break with the powers that hold a treasure so that others, not you, can have what they were hoarding. Ask whether your costliest break might be one made entirely for the good of those who can never repay it, and where God may be asking you to hand the light to people the gatekeepers overlooked.
upheaval.inTheBody: The gospel's light belongs to the simple, not to the scholars alone, and across history the Church has had to be reminded of it at great cost. William Tyndale vowed that the boy following a plow would know the Scriptures better than the learned clergy who kept them locked in Latin; forbidden to translate in England, he fled to the continent, produced the first printed English New Testament, and saw it smuggled home in bales of cloth past the men who would burn it. He was betrayed and burned near Brussels, his last breath spent praying that God would open the eyes of England's king. When the Body locks Scripture behind a guild, renewal breaks that lock, and the Word, once loosed, does not return void. His words filled the authorized English Bibles within the decade.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the Word that does not return empty. Translators are hunted and burned and the locks are thrown again and again, but the Scripture, once loosed, accomplishes what God sent it to do. The gatekeepers pass; the light they tried to hoard goes on giving understanding to the simple.
reflection: What have I been keeping under lock that was meant to be given away?
Am I willing to make a costly break for the sake of someone who can never repay me?
Where might God be asking me to hand the light to people the gatekeepers overlooked?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, You gave Your Word as light for the simple, not treasure for the few. Loosen my grip on what I was told to hoard. Make me willing to break, at cost, for the sake of others' access, trusting that what You send out does not return to You empty. Amen.

notes.primary: Psalm 119:130 (the entrance of your words gives light); Isaiah 55:11 (my word shall not return void).
notes.tradition: References William Tyndale (c. 1494–1536), the first printed English New Testament, his vow concerning the plowboy, and his dying prayer for the King of England; public domain, paraphrased.

title: The narrow way
moment: Some of the reformers looked at the Reformation and judged that it had stopped halfway. The break with Rome was real, but the new churches were still wedded to the magistrate, still baptizing every infant into a Christian society by default, still treating the whole of a territory as the people of God simply by birth. A smaller band could not accept it. They baptized one another again, as believing adults who had chosen the faith for themselves — and from that act came the name flung at them, Anabaptist, the re-baptizers. The church, they insisted, was meant to be a gathered people, voluntary, visibly distinct from the world around it, walking the narrow road on purpose. For this break within the break they were hunted without mercy. Catholics and Protestants, divided on nearly everything else, found common cause in destroying them; the radicals were imprisoned, exiled, drowned, and burned by both at once. They had pressed past the point where their own former allies would follow, onto the narrow way that few choose and fewer survive, and they paid for the second mile with their lives.
voiceQuote: How narrow is the gate, and restricted is the way that leads to life; few are those who find it.
scriptureText: You are an elect race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God's own possession, that you may show forth the excellencies of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light.
weight: Sometimes a first break, however brave, does not go far enough, and faithfulness asks a second one — lonelier than the first, because this time even your allies stay behind. The hardest disconnects are rarely the ones that win you a crowd. They are the ones that cost you the crowd you already had, the people who marched the first mile with you and will not walk the second. There is a real temptation, once a reform has won some ground, to settle at the comfortable halfway house and call the journey finished. The narrow way is narrow precisely because so few are willing to keep walking it after the easy applause runs out. Be careful, then, how you judge the ones who press on past where you stopped. They are sometimes simply more consistent than you, following the same logic further than your nerve allowed. The road that loses you even the approval of your friends is not, for that reason, the wrong road. It may be the most faithful mile of all.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect can come twice. Here the phase is the second, lonelier break — the one that presses past the point where former allies will follow. It asks whether you will keep walking the narrow road after the applause stops and the company thins, or settle at the comfortable halfway house and call the unfinished journey done.
upheaval.inYou: Sometimes your first break, however brave, does not go far enough, and faithfulness asks a second one, lonelier than the first, because this time even your allies stay behind. The hardest disconnects are rarely the ones that win you a crowd; they are the ones that cost you the crowd you already had, the people who marched the first mile with you and will not walk the second. There is a real temptation, once a reform has won some ground, to settle at the comfortable halfway house and call the journey finished. The narrow way is narrow precisely because so few keep walking it after the applause runs out. The road that loses you even the approval of your friends may be the most faithful mile of all.
upheaval.inTheBody: Renewal movements within the Church have a way of settling at a comfortable midpoint, and God raises up those who press on to the harder, fuller break. The Anabaptists judged that the Reformation had stopped halfway, still wedded to the magistrate and baptizing whole territories into a Christian society by default; they baptized one another as believing adults and insisted the Church was meant to be a gathered, voluntary people, visibly distinct from the world. For this second break within the break they were hunted by Catholic and Protestant alike, drowned and burned by both at once. The whole Body should be slow to destroy its radicals. The narrow-way people who walk past where the rest stopped are sometimes its most consistent and faithful, a holy nation God claims as His own.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the call to be a holy nation, a people God claims as His own, gathered and chosen rather than merely born into a crowd. Establishments harden and persecute and the company on the narrow road thins to almost none, but the people God sets apart for Himself remain His when every comfortable arrangement has fallen.
reflection: Where have I settled at a comfortable halfway point and called the journey finished?
Is there a second, lonelier break that faithfulness is asking of me, past where my allies will follow?
How do I treat the ones who press further than I dared — as fanatics, or as the more consistent?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I am tempted to stop at the easy halfway house and call it far enough. Give me courage for the second break when faithfulness requires it, even when my allies stay behind. Make me slow to condemn those who walk the narrow road further than I have dared. Amen.

notes.primary: Matthew 7:14 (narrow is the way); 1 Peter 2:9 (a holy nation, a people for God's own possession).
notes.tradition: References the Anabaptists and the radical Reformation (from c. 1525), believer's baptism, and their persecution by Catholics and Protestants alike; public domain, paraphrased.

title: Unless a grain dies
moment: Under Queen Mary, England is being dragged back to Rome, and the reformers who led it the other way are made to pay. Hugh Latimer, the old preacher, and Nicholas Ridley, the bishop, are brought to a ditch outside Oxford and bound back to back at a single stake. The fire is laid at their feet. As it is kindled, tradition records the words Latimer turns to give his friend — to be of good comfort and play the man, for on this day, by God's grace, they will light such a candle in England as he trusts shall never be put out. Then the flames take them. It is a terrible scene and a strangely confident one, two old men burning and speaking of light. They die, and the death is real; there is no pretending the fire was not fire. But it was also the thing Jesus described in the seed that must fall into the ground — the grain that goes down into the dark and dies and does not stay alone, but rises bearing much fruit. Mary's reign was short. The candle the fire was meant to extinguish outlasted the queen who lit it, and was not put out.
voiceQuote: Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.
scriptureText: I have fought the good fight. I have finished the course. I have kept the faith.
weight: The breaks that cost the most can be the most fruitful — not in spite of the dying, but precisely through it. This is the deepest and strangest law of the Kingdom, and it runs against every instinct you have. The grain that clutches at its own life, refusing to fall into the ground, keeps its life and stays alone, barren, a single seed forever. Only the one that goes down into the dark and lets itself be broken open comes up multiplied. So it is no accident that the church's seasons of fire have planted more than its seasons of ease ever managed. What you are tempted to read as pure loss — the thing in you that must die, the security that must fall, the comfort that must be surrendered for God's purpose to grow — may be the very seed going into the ground. The pattern does not change to spare you the dark. The fruit comes after the falling, never instead of it. Whatever must die in you for God's harvest, trust the order: down first, then up; the dark first, then the much fruit.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect reaches its strangest form here — the break that bears the most fruit precisely through the dying. The phase asks you to trust the seed's logic against every instinct: that what falls into the dark and is broken open is not lost but multiplied, and that the deepest fruitfulness lies on the far side of a real and costly death.
upheaval.inYou: The breaks that cost you the most can prove the most fruitful, not in spite of the dying but precisely through it. This is the deepest and strangest law of the Kingdom, and it runs against every instinct you have. The grain that clutches at its own life, refusing to fall into the ground, stays alone and barren, a single seed forever; only the one that goes down into the dark and lets itself be broken open comes up multiplied. What you are tempted to read as pure loss, the thing in you that must die, the comfort surrendered for God's purpose to grow, may be the very seed going into the ground. The pattern does not change to spare you the dark. Down first, then up; the dark first, then the much fruit.
upheaval.inTheBody: The Church's seasons of fire have planted more than its seasons of ease ever managed. Under Queen Mary, as England was dragged back to Rome, Hugh Latimer and Nicholas Ridley were bound back to back at a single stake outside Oxford, and tradition records Latimer's word to his friend, to be of good comfort and play the man, for that day they would light such a candle in England as he trusted should never be put out. The fire was real; the death was not pretended away. But it was the seed Jesus described, the grain that falls into the ground and does not stay alone. Mary's reign was short, and the candle the flames were meant to extinguish outlasted the queen who lit it.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the law of the falling seed itself. Queens burn the witnesses and the fires are real and the loss is not pretended away, but the grain that goes into the dark and dies comes up bearing much fruit. The candle they meant to extinguish outlives the hand that lit it.
reflection: What in me is being asked to fall into the ground and die for God's purpose to grow?
Am I clutching at a life that, kept, will only stay alone and barren?
Can I trust that the fruit comes after the falling, and not demand to see it first?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I would rather keep my life whole than let any grain of it fall into the dark. Teach me the seed's hard logic — that what dies in You is not lost but multiplied. Give me courage for the costly break, and faith that the fruit comes after the falling. Amen.

notes.primary: John 12:24 (unless a grain of wheat dies); 2 Timothy 4:7 (I have fought the good fight).
notes.tradition: References Hugh Latimer and Nicholas Ridley, burned at Oxford (1555), and Latimer's words about lighting a candle in England that would never be put out; public domain, paraphrased.

title: Strangers and pilgrims
moment: A small congregation of English Separatists had already done the hard thing once: they had broken from the national church to worship as they believed they must. It was not enough. To keep that worship they found they had to break from England itself, and then from their refuge in Holland, until the only ground left was an ocean and a wilderness on its far side. So in 1620 they crowded onto the Mayflower and pointed it west, toward a coast not one of them had seen. Picture what that crossing asked. They left language, kin, the graves of their dead, every familiar thing a person leans on, for a country that so far existed only as a hope. They were not adventurers chasing fortune. They were people who had decided that the freedom to worship as conscience demanded was worth becoming homeless for. The letter to the Hebrews had named them centuries before they sailed: those who confess that they are strangers and pilgrims on the earth, aliens in a land of promise, dwelling in tents, having seen from far off a homeland they do not yet hold. The break that crosses an ocean leaves a whole world behind for the sake of obedience.
voiceQuote: These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them and embraced them from afar, and having confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
voiceAttribution: The letter to the Hebrews — Hebrews 11:13 (WEB)
scriptureText: By faith he lived as an alien in the land of promise, as in a land not his own, dwelling in tents.
weight: Some breaks ask you to give up a little. Others ask you to pull up every root you have. You leave a place, a people, a whole settled life, and you do it not because anywhere better is waiting but because staying would mean betraying what God has asked of you. That is the pilgrim's break, and it is one of the hardest in this phase, because it strips away the very belonging that makes a person feel safe. If your obedience has made you a stranger somewhere, if following God has cost you the comfort of being at home, do not read that as a sign you took a wrong turn. It may be the surest sign you are walking in the oldest company of faith. The pilgrim accepts not belonging here, not because he loves exile, but because the homeland he is seeking lies elsewhere, and he has seen it from far enough off to leave everything else behind. You are not lost. You are on the road that all of them walked, looking for a country of your own.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect, at its most uprooting. The phase here asks whether you will leave not only what is wrong but what is dear and familiar, the whole comfortable world, for the sake of an obedience that makes you a stranger. It asks you to hold the homelessness honestly and to keep walking toward a homeland you have only seen from far off.
upheaval.inYou: Some breaks ask you to give up a little. Others ask you to pull up every root you have, leaving a place, a people, a whole settled life, and to do it not because anywhere better is waiting but because staying would mean betraying what God has asked of you. That is the pilgrim's break, one of the hardest, because it strips away the very belonging that makes a person feel safe. If your obedience has made you a stranger somewhere, if following God has cost you the comfort of home, do not read it as a sign you took a wrong turn. It may be the surest sign you walk in the oldest company of faith. You are not lost. You are on the road they all walked, looking for a country of your own.
upheaval.inTheBody: The Church is at its truest a pilgrim people, never fully at home in any land or age, ready to cross an ocean rather than betray conscience. The English Separatists had already broken from the national church once; to keep that worship they found they had to break from England itself, and then from their refuge in Holland, until the only ground left was an ocean and a wilderness beyond it, and in 1620 they pointed the Mayflower west toward a coast none of them had seen. The letter to the Hebrews had named the whole Body centuries before they sailed, those who confess they are strangers and pilgrims on the earth. When the Church grows too comfortably native to its culture, it has forgotten its own confession, that it is still seeking a country of its own.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the homeland itself. Lands and houses and the belonging they offer can all be left behind, and one day removed entirely. But the country the pilgrim seeks is the one that remains when everything shakable is gone, and the God who promised it does not move.
reflection: What roots is God asking me to pull up, and am I treating the cost as a wrong turn or as obedience?
Where have I grown so at home in my surroundings that I have forgotten I am a stranger on the earth?
What homeland am I actually living toward, and have I seen it clearly enough to leave lesser things behind?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, You have made me a stranger here, and some days the homelessness is heavy. Give me the pilgrim's heart that can let go of what is dear for the sake of obeying You. Keep my eyes on the homeland I have seen from far off, the country that cannot be shaken. Amen.

notes.primary: Hebrews 11:13-14 (strangers and pilgrims, seeking a homeland); Hebrews 11:9 (dwelling as an alien in tents).
notes.tradition: References the English Separatists / Pilgrims who sailed to the New World (1620) for freedom to worship; public domain history, paraphrased.

title: A heart strangely warmed
moment: By every outward measure John Wesley had arrived. He was an ordained priest of the Church of England, an Oxford man, the leader of a disciplined religious society, a missionary who had crossed the Atlantic and come home again. And by his own account he was cold. He had striven and failed, kept the rules and felt nothing, carried all the apparatus of faith with none of its fire. Then came an evening in 1738 that asked nothing of him but to sit and listen. At a meeting on Aldersgate Street someone was reading aloud Luther's preface to the letter to the Romans, and as the words moved through the room something gave way in the religious professional who had thought he had no further to go. He felt, as he later put it, his heart strangely warmed. For the first time he trusted Christ alone to save him, and knew the saving was done. The break, it turns out, can come even to the man who runs the meeting. The disconnect Wesley needed was not from heresy or scandal but from dead duty into living faith, the move from religion kept to a clean heart received. He had been creating nothing in himself; now it was created in him.
voiceQuote: Create in me a clean heart, God; renew a right spirit within me.
scriptureText: Not by works of righteousness which we did ourselves, but according to his mercy, he saved us, through the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit.
weight: You can be inside the faith for years and still need this break. You can serve, lead, teach, give, do everything right, and remain a stranger to the living thing underneath it all, running on duty and willpower and the quiet exhaustion of a heart that has never been warmed. If that is you, Wesley is good news, because he shows that it is never too late and no role too senior for the break from religion-as-performance into living trust. The most accomplished insider in the room can still be the one who most needs to be broken open. And notice the shape of it: the clean heart is not a wage you finally earn by enough effort. It is a gift you receive, often in the moment you stop striving and simply let the truth be read over you. If your faith has gone cold while your duties stayed warm, the answer is not to try harder at the performance. It is to let God create in you the thing you cannot manufacture, and to trust Christ alone for it.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect, turned inward. This is the break from dead religion into living faith, and the phase insists it can come even to the lifelong professional, the one who keeps every rule and feels nothing. It asks you to stop running on duty and willpower and to let the heart itself be broken open and warmed.
upheaval.inYou: You can be inside the faith for years and still need this break. You can serve, lead, teach, give, do everything right, and remain a stranger to the living thing underneath it all, running on duty and willpower and the quiet exhaustion of a heart that has never been warmed. If that is you, Wesley is good news, because he shows it is never too late and no role too senior for the break from religion-as-performance into living trust. The most accomplished insider in the room can still be the one who most needs to be broken open. The clean heart is not a wage you finally earn by enough effort. It is a gift you receive, often in the very moment you stop striving and let the truth be read over you.
upheaval.inTheBody: The Church can be full of competent religion and still be cold, its forms intact and its life quietly drained away, and its deepest renewals often begin when the professionals themselves are broken open into living faith. John Wesley had arrived by every outward measure, an ordained priest, an Oxford man, a missionary, and by his own account he was cold, carrying all the apparatus of faith with none of its fire. Then an evening in 1738 asked nothing of him but to sit and listen as Luther's preface to Romans was read aloud, and his heart was strangely warmed. A whole revival traced back to that one warmed heart. God has a habit of renewing the Body by first renewing its weary, dutiful insiders, the very people most sure they had no further to go.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the work that saves you, which was never yours to perform. Your cold seasons and your fervent ones rise and fall like weather. But Christ's finished mercy, the washing of regeneration you can only receive, holds steady beneath the changing temperature of your heart, and it does not depend on the strength of your striving.
reflection: Where am I running on duty and willpower, doing everything right while my heart stays cold?
Have I been trying to earn a clean heart as a wage rather than receiving it as a gift?
Do I secretly believe my role or experience puts me past the need for this kind of break?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have kept the rules and felt nothing, carrying the shape of faith without its fire. I cannot warm my own heart. Create in me a clean heart and renew a right spirit within me. Let me stop striving and simply trust Christ alone to save me, today. Amen.

notes.primary: Psalm 51:10 (create in me a clean heart); Titus 3:5 (saved by the washing of regeneration).
notes.tradition: References John Wesley's Aldersgate experience (1738), when his heart was strangely warmed; public domain, paraphrased.

title: Revive your work
moment: By the 1730s the churches of the American colonies had settled into a comfortable chill. The forms were intact, the pews filled on Sundays, the doctrine sound enough, and the life had quietly drained out of it all. Religion had become a thing inherited and managed rather than felt. Then something broke in that no one had scheduled. Under the searching preaching of Jonathan Edwards, who could hold a congregation over the edge of eternity until it trembled, and the open-air voice of George Whitefield, who preached to thousands in fields no church wall could hold, a great awakening swept across the land. People who had been nominally Christian their whole lives were jolted into something vivid and undone, weeping over sin they had never taken seriously, their settled lives reordered in a season. It looked less like a program than a flood. This is a kind of break the phase has to name, because it does not come by leaving. It comes by waking. Revival is a corporate disconnect, God breaking a sleeping church out of its own deadness, against the grain of its settled inertia. No committee voted for it. It arrived like weather, and the dry, formal religion it found could not stand in front of it.
voiceQuote: The LORD, I have heard of your fame; I stand in awe of your deeds. Renew your work in the midst of the years; in wrath, you remember mercy.
scriptureText: Won't you revive us again, that your people may rejoice in you?
weight: Sometimes the break you need is not to leave but to wake. You have not walked away from the faith; you have simply gone numb inside it, your love grown nominal, your prayers gone formal, the whole thing running on memory and habit. That sleep is its own kind of captivity, and you usually cannot shake yourself out of it by trying. Revival is God's disruptive mercy for exactly this, the in-breaking that jolts a cold heart awake against its own inertia. It is not always gentle, and it is rarely convenient, but it is mercy. And here is what you can do with a numb and sleepy faith: you can ask for the disruption. You can pray the prophet's prayer over your own cold heart, that God would renew His work in the midst of your years, that He would revive you again. You cannot manufacture the fire. But you can stop defending the sleep and start asking to be woken, which is the one move a slumbering heart is still free to make.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect, as awakening. Not every break is a leaving; this one is God breaking a sleeping church and a sleeping heart out of settled deadness, against their own inertia. The phase asks whether you will defend your numbness or ask to be woken, and whether you will let a disruption you cannot control reorder a faith gone formal.
upheaval.inYou: Sometimes the break you need is not to leave but to wake, to be jolted out of a faith gone nominal and sleepy into something alive again. Revival is God's disruptive mercy, and the one move a numb heart is still free to make is to ask for it. Pray the prophet's prayer over your own coldness: renew Your work, Lord, in the midst of my years.
upheaval.inTheBody: Churches calcify, and God has a long habit of breaking in with revival, awakening a sleeping body, often through unlikely preachers and against the establishment's comfort. A community can ask for this disruption, can pray to be revived again. The awakening is a break from deadness no church can manufacture or schedule, only seek and then make room for when it comes.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the God who revives. Fervor rises and cools, awakenings pass into memory, the warmest church can drift back toward sleep. But the One who breaks in to wake the dead is unchanged from age to age, and the work He renews in the midst of the years is His to keep alive, not ours.
reflection: Where has my faith gone numb and formal, running on habit and memory rather than life?
Am I defending my spiritual sleep, or am I willing to ask God to disrupt it?
What would it mean to pray honestly, renew Your work in the midst of my years, and then make room for the answer?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have gone cold inside a faith I never left, and I cannot wake myself. Break in with Your disruptive mercy. Renew Your work in the midst of my years, and revive me again, that I might rejoice in You. I stop defending the sleep and ask to be woken. Amen.

notes.primary: Habakkuk 3:2 (renew your work in the midst of the years); Psalm 85:6 (revive us again).
notes.tradition: References the Great Awakening (c. 1730s-40s), Jonathan Edwards and George Whitefield; public domain history, paraphrased.

title: Enlarge the tent
moment: He was a shoemaker who taught himself languages over his last, a country preacher of no great standing, and he had become convinced of something the church around him had quietly stopped believing: that the command to make disciples of all nations still stood, and the unreached peoples were waiting to hear. When the young William Carey pressed this on a gathering of ministers in 1792, an elder, by the account handed down, told him to sit down: if God meant to convert the heathen, He would do it without the likes of Carey. It was complacency speaking in the accent of piety, smallness calling itself trust in providence. Carey would not sit down. He pressed the church to expect great things from God and to attempt great things for God, and where others heard the limits of prudence he heard a tent whose cords had been left too short: enlarge the place of your tent, Isaiah had said, lengthen the cords, strengthen the stakes. So he founded a society and sailed for India, into a labor that would consume his life. His refusal to sit down shattered a complacency that had let the church forget the nations, and out of that one break the modern missionary movement was born.
voiceQuote: Enlarge the place of your tent... lengthen your cords, and strengthen your stakes.
scriptureText: How will they call on him in whom they have not believed? How will they believe in him whom they have not heard? And how will they hear without a preacher?
weight: Sometimes the break is simply being unwilling to sit down. Everyone around you has quietly accepted a smallness, a settled boundary on what God might do, a polite limit dressed up as wisdom and prudence and providence, and the upheaval God asks of you is to refuse it. That refusal will feel presumptuous, because complacency always sounds reasonable and the person who questions it always sounds like they are overreaching. Carey's disconnect was from exactly this: a comfortable smallness that everyone called prudence, a boundary no one had thought to question in years. And here is the cost the image of the tent makes plain. Enlarging it always means breaking the comfortable line of the stakes right where they are. You cannot lengthen the cords without pulling up the pegs that felt so settled and driving them out into ground that frightens you. If God is stirring you to attempt something larger than the room around you thinks reasonable, the break may be a holy one, the refusal to keep sitting down when grace is calling you to stand.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect, breaking outward. The phase here is not a turning inward but a refusal to keep the good news small, a break from a complacency that had decided the world need not be reached. It asks whether you will sit down with everyone else or pull up the comfortable stakes and let the tent be enlarged into ground that frightens you.
upheaval.inYou: Sometimes the break is being unwilling to sit down, refusing a complacency everyone around you has quietly accepted. Carey's disconnect was from a settled smallness that called itself prudence. If God is stirring you toward something larger than the room thinks reasonable, remember that enlarging the tent always means breaking the comfortable boundary of the stakes right where they are.
upheaval.inTheBody: Churches grow inward and forget the nations, dressing complacency as theology. God breaks that inertia through people who will not sit down, who insist the cords be lengthened and the stakes driven wider. The missionary break is the church refusing to keep the good news to itself, and a body that never produces such people has settled for a tent too small.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the reach of the gospel itself. Complacencies harden and are broken, boundaries are drawn and driven wider, but the command to carry the good news to all nations does not contract to fit a church's comfort. The mission stands when our settled smallness is shaken away, resting on the unchanging will of God.
reflection: What settled smallness around me have I quietly accepted as prudence rather than questioned as complacency?
Where is God stirring me to attempt something larger than the people around me think reasonable?
Which comfortable stakes is He asking me to pull up so the tent can be enlarged?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have grown comfortable inside boundaries I never questioned and called my smallness wisdom. Give me the holy refusal to sit down when You are calling me to stand. Help me expect great things from You and attempt great things for You, and to let the stakes be driven wider, wherever that leads. Amen.

notes.primary: Isaiah 54:2 (enlarge your tent); Romans 10:14 (how will they hear without a preacher?).
notes.tradition: References William Carey (1792), the modern missionary movement, and his call to expect and attempt great things for God; public domain, paraphrased.

title: Open your mouth
moment: In 1934 the official German church was bending to the Nazi state, remaking the gospel to fit a regime. To many it looked like loyalty. To a group of Christians who could not stomach it, it looked like a church selling its soul. They broke away to form what was called the Confessing Church, and at Barmen they set their refusal down in writing: the church has one Lord, Jesus Christ, and owes no rival allegiance to any earthly ruler or ideology. It was a line drawn through the heart of a captured institution. Among those who stood on the far side of it was a young pastor, Dietrich Bonhoeffer, who would give his short life to the resistance and pay for the break with his death. Mark what the disconnect was and was not. It was not a break over a fine point of doctrine. It was a break from a church that had fused itself to worldly power and called the fusion devotion, a refusal to be silent while the desolate were crushed. The mother of King Lemuel had charged her son to open his mouth for the mute, in the cause of all left desolate. At Barmen a remnant remembered that charge when the rest forgot it.
voiceQuote: Open your mouth for the mute, in the cause of all who are left desolate.
voiceAttribution: The mother of King Lemuel — Proverbs 31:8 (WEB)
scriptureText: To him who knows to do good, and doesn't do it, to him it is sin.
weight: There are breaks that conscience demands when the institution you belong to begins going along with evil. They are the costliest of all, because the pressure to stay is dressed as loyalty, and the people leaning on you to keep quiet are often the ones you most want to please. To open your mouth for those who cannot speak, to separate yourself from a comfortable complicity, can cost you your standing, your security, and, as it cost some at Barmen, your life. This is not a break to romanticize from a safe distance. It is meant to sober you. The temptation in such a moment is to tell yourself that silence is prudence, that staying inside lets you do more good, that the time to speak has not quite come. James cuts through all of it: to the one who knows to do good and does not do it, that failure is itself sin. Sometimes the only faithful move is the costly break, and the refusal to make it is not neutrality. It is the sin of knowing the good and declining to do it.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect, at its most costly. This is the break of conscience from a church co-opted by worldly power, the separation that may cost everything. The phase asks whether you will name complicity as complicity rather than loyalty, and whether you will open your mouth for the desolate even when silence is safer and the cost of speaking is real.
upheaval.inYou: There are breaks demanded by conscience when the institution you belong to goes along with evil. To open your mouth for those who cannot speak, to break from a comfortable complicity, can cost you everything. And silence is not the neutral safe ground it pretends to be. Knowing the good and refusing to do it, James says bluntly, is itself sin.
upheaval.inTheBody: The church is perpetually tempted to fuse with worldly power and call it loyalty. Sometimes faithfulness requires a costly break from a co-opted church, as at Barmen, where a remnant declared that Christ alone is Lord. A body that will not, when the moment comes, separate itself from complicity with evil has already lost the only Lord it claims to serve.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the church's one true Lord. Institutions bend to power and are exposed; allegiances that called themselves loyalty are torn away. But the lordship of Jesus Christ over His church does not yield to any earthly ruler or ideology, and it stands unmoved when every counterfeit devotion is shaken to the ground.
reflection: Where is an institution I belong to going along with something I know to be wrong?
Am I calling my silence prudence when conscience knows it is complicity?
Whom is God asking me to open my mouth for, even if speaking costs me dearly?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, when those around me fuse faith to power and call it loyalty, give me eyes to see it and courage to refuse it. Help me open my mouth for those who cannot speak, whatever it costs. Keep me from the sin of knowing the good and staying silent. You alone are Lord. Amen.

notes.primary: Proverbs 31:8 (open your mouth for the mute); James 4:17 (knowing the good and not doing it).
notes.tradition: References Dietrich Bonhoeffer and the Confessing Church's break from the Nazified German state church (the Barmen Declaration, 1934). Bonhoeffer's own writings are under copyright and are not quoted — only his actions and the historical events are referenced.

title: New things I declare
moment: We are living, by many accounts, inside one of the great upheavals that come round roughly every five hundred years. Phyllis Tickle named our version of it the Great Emergence, and likened the church to a house that periodically holds a giant rummage sale, clearing the attic of what no longer serves so the rooms can breathe again. From inside, it does not feel like housecleaning. It feels like the floor moving. The certainties of Christendom are cracking. Institutions that stood for generations are wobbling. A whole generation is laying its inherited faith out on the lawn, sorting, questioning, asking out loud where the authority finally lies. If you have felt the ground shift under the church you were raised in, you are not imagining it, and you are not alone in it. But the pattern is older than your fear. God has poured out His Spirit in such breaks before, on sons and daughters who thought the old world was ending. He is the kind of God who tells you of the new thing before it springs forth, while the former things are still falling. The shaking is loud. It is not, by itself, the end.
voiceQuote: It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy.
scriptureText: Behold, the former things have happened, and new things do I declare; before they spring forth I tell you of them.
weight: It changes things to know you were born into a hinge. Your private upheaval is real, and this does not shrink it, but it does set it inside something far larger than your own story. The doubts you carry, the church that disappointed you, the certainties that came apart in your hands, the sense that the whole edifice is groaning at once, you did not invent any of it alone in a room. You were handed a season. Whole eras of believers before you have stood exactly here, watching the old shell crack, terrified it meant the faith itself was failing. It did not. Every time, the cracking was the front edge of a renewal nobody in the rubble could yet see. That is not a promise that the institution you grew up in survives unchanged. Most of them did not. It is a promise about the One doing the shaking. Ask the steadying question underneath the panic: is what is falling the faith itself, or only the latest house the faith was living in? He declares new things before they spring forth. You are early in one of them.

upheaval.thePhase: This is Disconnect on the scale of an age. The phase asks you to stop reading the shaking of the church as its death certificate, and to recognize it instead as the painful opening of a renewal you cannot yet see. Disconnect, here, means trusting the pattern when the institutions crack: God has done this before.
upheaval.inYou: The break you are living is not only yours. You were set down inside a moment when the whole church is being shaken at once, and that is unsettling, but it means your small upheaval is folded into something vast that God is doing. The former things are passing. You are not watching the end. You are standing at a beginning.
