And into that vacancy comes the assignment, almost comically oversized for the group receiving it: you will be my witnesses, here in Jerusalem, then out into Samaria, the region they have been raised to distrust, and on to the very ends of the earth. Note the word He chooses. Not lawyers, not debaters, not winners of arguments. Witnesses, the kind of people who simply tell what they have seen. Years later Peter fills in the manner of it: always be ready to give a reason for the hope that is in you, but with humility and respect, never as a bludgeon swung to win. The reoriented life carries a hope worth explaining and is sent to explain it gently. You do not need every answer airtight. You need only be ready, when someone asks, to say honestly and without arrogance why the hope in you refused to die.
voiceQuote: You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.
scriptureText: Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear.
weight: Reorientation leaves you with something genuinely worth talking about: a hope that came through the wreckage and is still standing. But notice what Jesus does and does not ask of you. He sends witnesses, not experts; people who tell what they have seen, not people who win every argument. That should ease the dread many feel about speaking of their faith, the fear of being cornered by a question they cannot answer. You were never commissioned to be unbeatable in debate. Peter names the tone exactly: be ready to give a reason for your hope, but with humility and gentleness, never as a weapon to club someone into agreement. A bludgeon convinces no one; a witness, telling the truth kindly, disarms. So you do not need airtight answers before you are allowed to speak. You need only the readiness to say, when asked and gently, why the hope in you did not die in the storm that should have killed it. That much you can do, and it is enough.

upheaval.thePhase: Reorientation sends the rebuilt life out as a witness, not an arguer. See the small band on the hillside handed an enormous errand: be my witnesses to the ends of the earth. This phase is about telling what you have seen, with humility and respect, ready to give a reason for your hope but never wielding it as a weapon. The new bearings make you a gentle teller, not a debater out to win.
upheaval.inYou: You may dread speaking of your faith, afraid of the question you cannot answer, braced to be cornered and lose. Hear what Jesus actually asks of you. He sends witnesses, not experts, people who simply tell what they have seen, not people who win every argument. That should ease the dread, because you were never commissioned to be unbeatable in debate. Peter names the tone exactly: be ready to give a reason for your hope, but with humility and gentleness, never as a weapon to club someone into agreement. A bludgeon convinces no one; a witness, telling the truth kindly, disarms. So you do not need airtight answers before you may speak. You need only the readiness to say, when asked and gently, why the hope in you refused to die in the storm that should have killed it.
upheaval.inTheBody: The Church can mistake witness for winning, broadcasting at the world rather than testifying to it, and the temptation has recurred in every age of Christian confidence. Jesus commissioned witnesses, ordinary people who tell what they have seen, and sent them from Jerusalem to Samaria, the region they had been raised to distrust, and on to the very ends of the earth. Peter insisted on humility and respect in the telling. The Body's most fruitful seasons have looked less like winning arguments and more like a credible, gentle account of a hope that came through wreckage still breathing. Before a watching world the Church testifies most truly not when it dominates the room but when it points, humbly and without arrogance, to what it has actually seen of God.
upheaval.whatRemains: Arguments are lost, and even the best account of your hope can fall on deaf ears. What cannot be shaken is the thing you witnessed, the hope that came through your own wreckage still breathing. Your eloquence may fail and your answers run out, but what you have actually seen of God stands, and no unanswered question can unsay it.
reflection: Do I think I must win the argument before I am allowed to speak of my hope?
When I talk about my faith, is my tone a witness or a weapon?
What is the one true thing I have seen that I could simply, gently, tell?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, You sent ordinary people as witnesses, not as debaters who must win. Take from me the fear that I need every answer before I can speak. Make me ready to give a reason for my hope, but always with humility and gentleness, never as a bludgeon. Let me simply tell what I have seen of You, and trust that the truth, told kindly, is enough. Amen.

notes.primary: Acts 1:8 (you will be my witnesses to the ends of the earth); 1 Peter 3:15 (ready to give a reason for your hope, with humility).

title: Tell what He has done
moment: A man who has terrified an entire region sits quietly in the grass. For as long as anyone can remember he has lived among the tombs, naked, gashing himself with stones, screaming through the nights so that the whole shoreline learned to keep away. Chains never held him. Now he is dressed, calm, in his right mind, sitting at the feet of the One who set him free. And he asks the obvious thing: let me come with You. Jesus says no, and hands him instead an assignment harder and humbler than discipleship on the road. Go home, He says, to your own people, to the very ones who knew you at your worst, and tell them what the Lord has done for you, and how He had mercy on you. No theology degree. No sermon. Just the story, his own: this is how I was, and this is what He did. The psalmist had called for exactly this centuries before, let the redeemed of the LORD say so. Reorientation hands you a testimony for one simple reason. You have a before, and you have an after. And a changed person plainly telling their own true story is the most disarming witness there is.
voiceQuote: Go to your house, to your friends, and tell them what great things the Lord has done for you, and how he had mercy on you.
voiceAttribution: Jesus, to the healed man — Mark 5:19 (WEB)
scriptureText: Let the redeemed of the LORD say so, whom he has redeemed from the hand of the adversary.
weight: You may be certain you have nothing to offer as a witness, no training, no eloquence, no gift for words. The man among the tombs had none of that either, and Jesus sent him out anyway with the simplest assignment imaginable: go home and tell them what the Lord has done for you. Not what He has done in general. What He has done for you. That is the testimony no one can argue you out of, because it is not a position to be debated but a life that was changed. Be careful, though, of one quiet lie: that what God did in your upheaval was too small or too ordinary to mention. The honest before-and-after of your own story, told plainly to the people who knew you before, reaches places no polished argument can touch. The redeemed, the psalm says, should simply say so. So say so. Not impressively. Just truthfully, to the ones who remember who you were, this is how I was, and this is what He did.

upheaval.thePhase: Reorientation turns your own history into testimony. See the formerly tormented man, now calm, sent not on the road but back to his own town to tell his story. This phase needs no eloquence and no expertise, only the honest before-and-after of a changed life. The new bearings hand you a testimony precisely because you now have a before and an after worth telling.
upheaval.inYou: You may be certain you have nothing to offer as a witness, no training, no eloquence, no gift for words. The man among the tombs had none of that either, and Jesus sent him out anyway with the simplest assignment imaginable: go home and tell them what the Lord has done for you. Not what He has done in general, but what He has done for you. That is testimony no one can argue you out of, because it is not a position to debate but a life that was changed. Be careful of one quiet lie, that what God did in your upheaval was too small to mention. The honest before-and-after of your own story, told plainly to the people who knew you before, reaches places no argument can touch. So say so, not impressively, just truthfully.
upheaval.inTheBody: The Church can outsource witness to professionals and platforms, forgetting that across the centuries its most disarming testimony has been ordinary people telling their own stories. Jesus sent the healed man back to his own town with nothing but what had happened to him, and that pattern has carried Christianity further than any strategy: the redeemed, simply saying so. The movements that spread fastest were rarely the most polished; they were the ones where changed lives were freely recounted and the psalm's charge was taken at its word, let the redeemed of the LORD say so. Before a watching world the Body discovers again and again that a life genuinely changed is hard to wave away, and that everyone with a before-and-after has something worth telling.
upheaval.whatRemains: Memories fade and skeptics dismiss, but a life that was actually changed is hard to wave away. What cannot be shaken is what the Lord truly did for you, the real before and the real after that no counterargument can undo. Your account may be doubted, but the change itself happened, and the One who worked it does not unwork it.
reflection: What is the honest before-and-after that the Lord has worked in my own life?
Have I dismissed my story as too small or too ordinary to be worth telling?
Who are the people who knew me before, to whom I could simply say so?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, You did not require the eloquence of the man among the tombs, only his story. Take from me the lie that what You did in me is too small to mention. Give me courage to go to the people who knew me before and tell them, plainly, what You have done and how You had mercy on me. Let the redeemed simply say so. Amen.

notes.primary: Mark 5:19 (go home and tell what the Lord has done for you); Psalm 107:2 (let the redeemed say so).

title: An anchor for the soul
moment: A ship is caught out in the dark, far from any harbor, pitching and rolling as the sea heaves under it and the wind tears at the rigging. Nothing on the surface is calm; nothing on the surface can be trusted. And the one thing keeping the vessel off the rocks is invisible from the deck: an anchor, dropped far down through the black water, its fluke buried in solid ground beneath all the chaos, holding the ship fast to something that does not move. The letter to the Hebrews reaches for precisely this image. We have this hope, it says, as an anchor of the soul, both sure and steadfast. Weigh the words carefully. Not hope as a wish, a maybe, a hopeful crossing of the fingers that the weather will improve. Hope as an anchor, fastened to something solid below the surface, holding the soul steady while the waves still break overhead. The hope reaches, the letter goes on, into the very inner place where Christ has already gone. Reorientation never promised the storms were finished. What it gives is an anchor for the storms still to come, and a God of hope who fills you with enough joy and peace to ride them out.
voiceQuote: This hope we have as an anchor of the soul, a hope both sure and steadfast.
voiceAttribution: The letter to the Hebrews — Hebrews 6:19 (WEB)
scriptureText: Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that you may abound in hope, in the power of the Holy Spirit.
weight: Hear this clearly, because it guards you against a cruel disappointment: reorientation does not promise calm seas ahead. The rebuilt life still meets weather. What you are given is not a forecast of fair skies but an anchor for the storms that will surely come. And Christian hope, the kind Hebrews names, is not wishful optimism, not a sunny feeling that everything will probably work out. It is an anchor of the soul, sure and steadfast, fastened to something beneath the chaos that simply does not move. So when the surface of your life heaves again, and it will, the anchor holds, not because you happen to feel hopeful that day, but because the hope itself is fixed to Christ, who has already gone ahead into the solid ground where it grips. Feelings rise and fall with the swell. The anchor holds regardless. Ask the God of hope, then, not to still every storm, but to fill you with joy and peace enough to ride the next one out, held fast to ground that cannot shift.

upheaval.thePhase: Reorientation hands you an anchor, not a promise of calm seas. See the ship in the storm and the unseen anchor buried in solid ground beneath the chaos: that is the hope this phase gives. Not wishful optimism that the weather will improve, but a sure and steadfast hold fastened to Christ below the surface. The new bearings steady you for storms still to come rather than promising they are over.
upheaval.inYou: You may be waiting for reorientation to deliver calm seas at last. It does not. What it gives you is an anchor for the storms still ahead. Christian hope is not wishful optimism, not a sunny feeling that everything will probably work out; it is an anchor of the soul, sure and steadfast, dropped through the black water and buried in solid ground beneath the chaos. So when the surface of your life heaves again, and it will, the anchor holds, not because you feel hopeful that day but because the hope itself is fastened to Christ, who has already gone ahead into the ground where it grips. Ask the God of hope not to still every storm, but to fill you with joy and peace enough to ride the next one out.
upheaval.inTheBody: The Church can hand its people a cheerful optimism that snaps in the first real gale, mistaking a sunny mood for hope, and every age that has done so has watched faith founder when the weather turned. The hope the letter to the Hebrews describes is sturdier and belongs to the whole Body: an anchor, sure and steadfast, fastened to Christ beneath the chaos, reaching into the very inner place where He has already gone. Through every storm of history, persecution, plague, collapse, the Church has not been promised calm seas but given a real anchor and pointed to the God of hope. Before a watching world a hope like that holds Christ's people steady precisely when the storm has not yet passed, buried in unshakable ground that does not drag.
upheaval.whatRemains: Storms return, and the surface of a life can heave for a long time before it stills. What cannot be shaken is the ground the anchor grips, the inner place where Christ has already gone ahead. The waves are real and the night is long, but the hold is fastened to One who does not move, and an anchor buried in unshakable ground does not drag.
reflection: Have I been waiting for calm seas instead of receiving an anchor for the storms still to come?
Is my hope a feeling that rises and falls, or something fastened to Christ beneath the chaos?
When the surface of my life heaves, what am I actually holding on to?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I confess I keep hoping for calm seas, and grow afraid when the storms return. Thank You that You gave me not fair weather but an anchor, sure and steadfast, fastened to Christ where the ground does not move. When my life heaves again, hold me fast. Fill me, God of hope, with joy and peace enough to ride out the storm, trusting the anchor even when I cannot see it. Amen.

notes.primary: Hebrews 6:19 (hope as an anchor of the soul); Romans 15:13 (the God of hope fill you).

title: Not worth comparing
moment: Picture an old balance scale, the kind with two brass pans hanging from a beam. Into the first pan, load the present sufferings, and do not lighten the load to make a point: the chronic pain, the buried child, the marriage that ended, the years lost to illness or grief. Paul knew the weight of that pan. He was flogged until his back was open, stoned and left for dead, shipwrecked, hungry, cold, betrayed. He never once pretends the pan is empty. Then he loads the other pan. Onto it he sets the glory that is coming, the unveiling of everything God has been preparing, and when it lands the beam swings hard and the first pan flies upward, not because the suffering weighed nothing but because the glory weighs so much more. That is the only sense in which Paul calls his afflictions not worth comparing. He is not telling the wounded to cheer up, and he is not lightening the load he himself carried. He is doing the math of eternity out loud, watching the scale tip past the edge of comparison entirely.
voiceQuote: The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which will be revealed toward us.
scriptureText: For our light affliction, which is for the moment, works for us more and more exceedingly an eternal weight of glory.
weight: Hear this gently, because it can be twisted into a weapon: you are not being told your pain is small. Paul, who suffered as much as almost anyone in Scripture, never calls present suffering light in itself. He calls it light only against an eternal weight of glory so vast the scale tips out of all comparison. Those are different claims, and the difference is everything. The ache you carry right now is real, and naming it is not a lack of faith. What reorientation gives you is not a denial of the ache but a longer view of it, the refusal to let what hurts now stand as the whole story or the final word. Hold both at once. Let your present grief be honest and unhurried, never bullied into silence, and let the coming glory be real enough to lean on. What is coming will outweigh what is hurting, immeasurably, and it will do so without ever pretending the hurt away.

upheaval.thePhase: Reorientation hands you the long view: present suffering set against coming glory, never minimized, only outweighed. Watch Paul load both pans of the scale honestly, refusing to empty the pan of pain and still watching the glory swing the beam. This phase does not rush you past the ache; it teaches you to see it inside a far larger frame, where what is coming dwarfs what is hurting without erasing a single tear of it.
upheaval.inYou: This is no command to belittle what you carry. Picture an old balance scale, and into the first pan load your present sufferings without lightening them, the chronic pain, the buried child, the marriage that ended, the years lost to grief. Paul knew the weight of that pan; he was flogged, stoned, shipwrecked, and never once pretends it empty. Then he loads the other pan with the glory that is coming, and the beam swings hard, not because your suffering weighs nothing but because the glory weighs so much more. That is the only sense in which he calls affliction not worth comparing. Reorientation gives you not denial of the ache but a longer view of it. So hold both: let your present grief be honest and unhurried, and let the coming glory be real enough to lean on.
upheaval.inTheBody: The Church can swing coming glory like a club to silence present grief, hurrying the bereaved past their tears with talk of heaven, and in every age that misuse has wounded the very people it claimed to comfort. Paul does no such thing. He honors the full weight of real suffering, the pan loaded and never emptied, and only then sets it against a far greater weight of glory until the scale tips past all comparison. The Body at its truest weeps truthfully now and still keeps the long view, naming the ache without minimizing it. Before a watching world the Church is most honest when it neither denies present sorrow nor lets it stand as the final word, telling the truth that what is coming will outweigh what hurts.
upheaval.whatRemains: Pain is real, and it is not the measure of things. What cannot be shaken is the glory God is preparing, an eternal weight set on the far pan of the scale, so heavy that every present sorrow, fully felt and never denied, is finally outweighed by what is coming.
reflection: Where have I let present pain quietly become the whole and final story of my life?
Can I name my ache honestly and still trust that a greater weight of glory is coming?
Have I ever used coming glory to silence someone's grief instead of sitting with it?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, the pain is real, and You have never asked me to pretend it small. Let me name it honestly before You. And set it, in Your time, against the weight of glory You are preparing, until the scale tips past all comparison. Hold both in me, the honest ache and the coming joy, and steady me with the longer view. Amen.

notes.primary: Romans 8:18 (present sufferings not worth comparing to coming glory); 2 Corinthians 4:17 (light affliction, eternal weight of glory).

title: Love casts out fear
moment: There is a sound the old life made, so constant you stopped hearing it: a low hum of fear running underneath everything. Fear of not being enough. Fear of being found out. Fear of the dropped mask, the failed grade, the withdrawn approval, the punishment you were sure was owed. It drove the striving and the hiding both, the long hours and the careful editing of yourself, the bracing for a blow that always seemed about to fall. John, the old apostle who had leaned on Jesus at the table, names the one thing strong enough to evict that hum. There is no fear in love, he writes, and perfect love casts out fear, because fear has to do with punishment. Picture it as a tenant being put out: love moves in, and the dread that had squatted in every room for years finally drains out the door. The perfectly loved are not bracing for a blow. They have stopped listening for the footsteps on the stair. Paul says it from his own cell: God did not give us a spirit of fear, but of power and love and a sound mind.
voiceQuote: There is no fear in love; but perfect love casts out fear.
scriptureText: For God didn't give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.
weight: So much of the old life ran on fear, and you may not have noticed because it was always there, the way you stop hearing a noise that never stops. Fear of failing, of exposure, of punishment, of being finally rejected once someone saw the real you. John names the single force that evicts it, and it is not willpower or positive thinking. It is being loved. Perfect love casts out fear, he says, because love like that has no punishment waiting inside it. The more deeply you come to know yourself loved by God, not tolerated, not on probation, but truly loved, the more the old dread loses its footing and drains away. You were not handed a spirit of fear in the first place, and you are not required to live under one now. Let the perfect love of God move into the very rooms where fear has been living rent-free for years, and do not be surprised when the old terror finally has nowhere left to stand.

upheaval.thePhase: Reorientation slowly evicts the fear that drove the old life. Hear John name it: perfect love casts out fear, because fear is bound up with punishment, and the perfectly loved are not bracing for a blow. This phase does not just manage the old dread; it crowds it out by moving the soul deeper into a love with no punishment in it, until the hum that ran everything finally falls silent.
upheaval.inYou: So much of your old life ran on fear, and you may not have noticed because it was always there, the way you stop hearing a noise that never stops. Fear of failing, of exposure, of punishment, of being finally rejected once someone saw the real you. John names the single force that evicts it, and it is not willpower; it is being loved. Perfect love casts out fear, he says, because love like that has no punishment waiting inside it. The more deeply you know yourself loved by God, not tolerated, not on probation, but truly loved, the more the old dread loses its footing and drains away. You were never handed a spirit of fear, and you need not live under one now. Let His perfect love move into the rooms where fear has lived rent-free.
upheaval.inTheBody: The Church can run on fear, of judgment, of exclusion, of never quite measuring up, and mistake the resulting compliance for faith, a danger that has shadowed Christianity in every age it has preferred control to grace. John exposes it for the whole Body: perfect love casts out fear, and where dread still rules, love has not yet been made complete. The renewals that have brought the Church back to life have led with the love of God rather than the threat of punishment, and discovered that a people freed from fear serve from love rather than terror. Before a watching world, fear breeds hiders and perfect love sets free children, and the Body is most itself when it offers the world a love with no punishment in it.
upheaval.whatRemains: Fear can be made to look like reverence, but it was never the foundation. What cannot be shaken is a love with no punishment in it, a love that does not tolerate or merely permit you but holds you, and into which the old dread cannot follow.
reflection: What fear has hummed under my life so long that I have stopped noticing it is there?
Do I relate to God as One loved by, or as One I am still bracing to be punished by?
Where would my choices change if I truly believed the love holding me has no punishment in it?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, You did not give me a spirit of fear, yet fear has lived in me for years, driving the striving and the hiding. Move Your perfect love into every room where dread has squatted. Let me know myself loved by You, not tolerated, not on probation, but loved, until the old terror has nowhere left to stand. Cast it out, and make me free. Amen.

notes.primary: 1 John 4:18 (perfect love casts out fear); 2 Timothy 1:7 (not a spirit of fear, but of power and love).

title: Nothing can separate
moment: Watch a man in a borrowed room dictate a sentence as if he were daring the whole universe to defeat it. Paul begins to build a list, and he builds it like a fortress wall, stone on stone. Death, he says, and then life, as though to leave nothing on either side of the grave. Angels, then rulers, the seen powers and the unseen. Things present, things to come, the whole anxious weight of the future thrown onto the pile. Powers, height, depth, the dizzy top and the dark bottom of all existence. And then, in case some clever enemy is still searching for the one loophole, he sweeps the whole of reality into a single phrase and slams the gate: nor any other created thing. None of it, he concludes, can separate us from the love of God in Christ. Jesus had already said the same in a quieter key, holding up His open hand: my sheep are here, and no one is able to snatch them out. After an upheaval that shook loose everything that could be shaken, the soul finally finds the floor, and the floor is a grip that will not let go.
voiceQuote: Neither death, nor life... will be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
scriptureText: I give eternal life to them. They will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.
weight: After everything that came loose in your upheaval, here is bedrock, and it is worth standing on slowly. Nothing can separate you from the love of God in Christ. Paul does not leave the claim vague; he names every candidate one by one. Death. Life. Powers you can see and powers you cannot. The future you dread. And then, in case he missed one, anything that has ever been created at all. He rules them out, every one. Jesus puts it in your hands as an image: you are held, and no one is strong enough to tear you out of His grip. Notice where your security actually rests. It is not your grip on God, which trembles and slips on your worst days, the days you cannot feel Him at all. It is His grip on you, which does not slip on any day. That is the whole difference. Rest there. The cord that holds you was never yours to keep tight. It cannot be cut.

upheaval.thePhase: Reorientation settles the soul onto the security of being held. Watch Paul dare the universe with his list and rule out every separator, then hear Jesus hold up the hand no one can pry open. This phase is not the thrill of a tighter grip on God but the deeper rest of His unbreakable grip on you, the moment the shaken soul stops white-knuckling and discovers it was being carried all along.
upheaval.inYou: After everything that came loose in your upheaval, here is bedrock, and it is worth standing on slowly: nothing can separate you from the love of God in Christ. Paul does not leave the claim vague; he names every candidate one by one. Death. Life. Powers you can see and powers you cannot. The future you dread. And then, in case he missed one, anything created at all. He rules them out, every one. Jesus puts it in your hands as an image: you are held, and no one can tear you out of His grip. Notice where your security actually rests. It is not your grip on God, which slips on your worst days; it is His grip on you, which does not slip on any day. Rest there. The cord that holds you cannot be cut.
upheaval.inTheBody: The Church can leave its people endlessly anxious about their standing, never quite sure they are safe, and in every age a fearful Christianity has bred striving instead of rest. Paul's thunderous list and Jesus' image of the unbreakable hand answer that dread head on for the whole Body: nothing in all creation can separate the people of God from His love. Through persecution, exile, and collapse, the truth has held across the centuries, that the security of Christ's people is not their fragile grip on God but His grip on them. Before a watching world the Church serves from security rather than fear precisely when it has grasped this, a people who know they cannot be snatched away from the love that took hold of them at the cross.
upheaval.whatRemains: Everything else in the upheaval came loose; this did not. What cannot be shaken is the grip of God on you, a hold no death or power or unknown future can pry open, a love from which no created thing in all the universe can tear you away.
reflection: Which item on Paul's list, death, the future, some power, do I most fear could separate me from God?
Am I trusting my grip on God to keep me, or His grip on me?
What changes on my worst day if my security rests on being held rather than on holding on?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, so much came loose in the shaking, but You did not. Death, life, the powers, the future I cannot see, none of them can separate me from Your love in Christ. When my own grip on You slips, remind me that I am held by Yours, and Yours does not slip. Let me rest in the hand no one can pry open. The cord cannot be cut. Amen.

notes.primary: Romans 8:38-39 (nothing can separate us from God's love); John 10:28 (no one snatches them from my hand).

title: The greatest of these
moment: Come to the end of the most famous lines ever written about love, the lines read at half the weddings in the world, and notice what Paul does once the soaring is done. He has said love is patient and kind, that it bears all things and believes all things and never fails. And now, at the close, he sets three survivors on the table like the last three figures standing after everything else has been cleared away. Faith. Hope. Love. Three things that remain. And then he does something almost startling: he ranks them. The greatest of these, he says, is love. Sit with why. Faith will one day become sight, the believing swallowed up in seeing the One believed in. Hope will be swallowed up in having, every longing finally answered. But love does not get retired when the others are fulfilled. Love simply goes on, into the life of the world to come, the one thing that outlasts even faith and hope themselves. Colossians reaches for a different picture, a wardrobe: put on love over everything else, it says, the outer garment that holds the whole outfit together.
voiceQuote: Now remain faith, hope, and love, these three. The greatest of these is love.
scriptureText: Above all these things, walk in love, which is the bond of perfection.
weight: After all the rebuilding, the recovered beliefs, the hard-won hope, the slow relearning of how to trust, reorientation comes finally to rest on the one thing that outlasts the rest. Love. Faith will turn to sight; hope will be swallowed up in having; but love simply goes on. Paul ranks it greatest of the three, and Colossians says to pull it on over everything else like a coat. Here is the warning hidden in the comfort. It is dangerously possible to rebuild a faith centered on being right, on having finally sorted out the correct positions, on winning the argument you lost in your old life. A reconstructed certainty can be a hard and loveless thing. Do not let the center of your rebuilt life be rightness. Let it be love. You can be right about a great many things and still have missed the very center, because love is what remains, and love is what was greatest all along, even when you were too busy being correct to notice.

upheaval.thePhase: Reorientation comes to rest on its true center, and the center is love. Watch Paul end the great poem by ranking three survivors and crowning the last: faith becomes sight, hope is fulfilled, but love goes on. This phase is not finally about arriving at the right answers; it is about a rebuilt life ordered around love, the one thing that outlasts every conviction and holds the whole reconstructed self together.
upheaval.inYou: After all the rebuilding, the recovered beliefs, the hard-won hope, the slow relearning of trust, reorientation comes finally to rest on the one thing that outlasts the rest: love. Faith will one day turn to sight, the believing swallowed up in seeing the One believed in; hope will be swallowed up in having, every longing answered; but love simply goes on, into the life of the world to come. Here is the warning hidden in the comfort. It is dangerously possible to rebuild a faith centered on being right, on having sorted out the correct positions, on winning the argument you lost in your old life. Do not let the center of your rebuilt life be rightness. Let it be love, because you can be right about a great many things and still have missed the very center.
upheaval.inTheBody: The Church can prize correct doctrine or vibrant hope and quietly demote love to an afterthought, even a casualty, and the history of Christianity is scarred where it has done exactly that, right in its convictions and empty of charity. Paul will not allow it for the whole Body: of faith, hope, and love, the greatest is love, the one that does not get retired when the others are fulfilled but goes on into the life of the world to come. The reformations and renewals that endured put love on over everything, letting it be the bond that holds the rest together. Before a watching world a Church right about everything yet loveless has missed the very center, for love is what remains, and what was always greatest.
upheaval.whatRemains: Beliefs will be confirmed and longings answered, and even faith and hope will one day have done their work. What cannot be shaken is love, the survivor of the three, the one thing that does not get retired when the others are fulfilled but simply goes on into the life of the world to come.
reflection: Have I rebuilt a faith centered on being right rather than on love?
If faith becomes sight and hope is fulfilled, what would it mean to live now for the love that outlasts them?
Where am I winning arguments while quietly losing the very thing Paul calls greatest?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have worked hard to rebuild, and somewhere along the way I began to prize being right more than loving well. Forgive me. Faith will become sight and hope will be fulfilled, but love goes on, and love is what You call greatest. Make it the center of my rebuilt life. Help me put it on over everything else, until it is the thing that remains in me. Amen.

notes.primary: 1 Corinthians 13:13 (faith, hope, love; the greatest is love); Colossians 3:14 (above all, put on love).

title: I have kept the faith
moment: An old man sits in a cold Roman cell with the executioner's date already set, and picks up a pen to write his last surviving letter. He does not waste the page on regret or on settling scores. Instead, like a runner gasping out a few words at the tape, he writes three short clauses that carry the weight of a whole life: I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. Listen to the strange peace in them. He does not say he won every argument, or that nothing ever shook him, or that he never doubted in the dark. He says he kept the faith. He held on, all the way through, to the end. This is the summit toward which reorientation has been climbing: not a faith that never breaks, but a faith strong enough to be kept. And the secret of the keeping is not in the grip of his own clenched fist. It is in his gaze. Hebrews names it, looking to Jesus, the author and finisher of faith, who endured His own cross for the joy set before Him and finishes what He begins. From this height the finish line is finally in view, though the road still runs on past the ridge.
voiceQuote: I have fought the good fight. I have finished the course. I have kept the faith.
scriptureText: Looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising shame.
weight: Reorientation has been rebuilding you toward exactly this. The goal was never a faith that never breaks. It was a faith you can keep, all the way to the end. Paul, with death at the door, did not boast that he had won every argument or stood unshaken through every storm. He said he had kept the faith, held on through everything, and there is more peace in that than in any record of victories. That is the goal of your new bearings too. And here is the secret that takes the pressure off: the keeping does not finally depend on your grip, which has slipped before and will again. It depends on your gaze. You keep the faith by looking to the One who authors it and finishes it, who started this in you and has promised to complete it. From here you can see the finish line, but hear this clearly: you see it; you have not yet crossed it. The road still runs on, and the summit only shows how far the faithfulness reaches. So fix your eyes on Jesus, and keep walking.

upheaval.thePhase: Reorientation reaches its summit here, the finish line at last in view. Watch the old runner gasp out his three clauses, and notice the goal was never a faith that cannot break but one strong enough to be kept. This phase climbs to a height from which you finally see how far the faithfulness reaches, eyes fixed on Jesus, the author and finisher. It is a ridge with the goal in sight, not the journey's end, for the road runs on.
upheaval.inYou: Reorientation has been rebuilding you toward exactly this. The goal was never a faith that never breaks; it was a faith you can keep, all the way to the end. Paul, with death at the door, did not boast that he had won every argument or stood unshaken through every storm. He said he had kept the faith, held on through everything, and there is more peace in that than in any record of victories. And the secret takes the pressure off: the keeping depends not on your grip, which has slipped before, but on your gaze, on looking to the One who authors and finishes faith, who began this in you and promises to complete it. The finish line is in view, but you have not yet crossed it. So fix your eyes on Jesus, and keep walking.
upheaval.inTheBody: The Church can aim at being impressive, or unshakeable, and miss the humbler, sturdier goal that has carried Christianity across the centuries: a faith strong enough to be kept, all the way home. Paul's finish-line words name it for the whole Body, fought, finished, kept. Through every shaking of history the Church has endured not because it never bent but because generation after generation fixed its eyes on Jesus, the author and finisher of faith, who endured His own cross for the joy set before Him and finishes what He begins. Before a watching world the Body proves faithful not by never breaking but by being kept, walking the long road with its gaze fixed on the One who sees the faith of His people through to the end.
upheaval.whatRemains: Arguments will be won and lost, and storms will come that shake a great deal loose. What cannot be shaken is the One who authors faith and finishes it, Jesus, who started this in you and will see it kept all the way to the end you can now begin to see.
reflection: Have I been chasing a faith that never breaks instead of one strong enough to be kept?
When my grip on God slips, where am I fixing my gaze?
What would change if I lived as someone with the finish line finally in view, but still on the road?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I once wanted a faith that could never break; teach me instead a faith I can keep. Like Paul, let me one day say I fought, I finished, I held on. The keeping is not in my grip but in my gaze, so fix my eyes on Jesus, the author and finisher of faith. The finish line is in view. Keep me walking the road that still runs on. Amen.

notes.primary: 2 Timothy 4:7 (I have finished the course, kept the faith); Hebrews 12:2 (looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith).

title: Christ in you
moment: Paul is writing from a cell, chains on his wrists, and he is circling something he calls a mystery, a secret kept hidden for ages and generations. Watch how he builds to it. He could be about to unveil a hidden rule, a system, a key that unlocks the universe. The Colossians lean in. And when he finally names the secret at the center of everything, it turns out not to be a thing at all, but a Person, and not a Person far off, but startlingly near: Christ in you, the hope of glory. Sit with the small word that carries the whole weight. Not Christ above you, supervising from a height. Not Christ beside you, walking alongside like a companion who could one day part ways. Christ in you. The living Lord taking up residence in the actual interior of an ordinary, chained, unremarkable life. The whole long road of the upheaval, every breaking and wandering and slow relearning, has been clearing the ground for exactly this. Of all the things a shaken soul might reconnect to, the one that matters most is not a doctrine or a building or even a recovered faith. It is the One who has moved in.
voiceQuote: Christ in you, the hope of glory.
scriptureText: I in them, and you in me, that they may be perfected into one; that the world may know that you sent me, and loved them, even as you loved me.
weight: After everything you have rebuilt, here is the reconnection that holds the rest in place, and it is not first to a church, a creed, or even a returning faith. It is to Christ Himself, alive inside you. Let that land plainly: He is not watching from above, deciding whether you measure up. He is not merely walking beside you, near but separate. He is in you, the way life is in a living thing. And notice what your hope of glory is now staked on. Not your performance, which the storm exposed. Not your recovered certainty, which still flickers. Your hope is the living Christ, taking up residence in the interior of your one ordinary life. This is union, and the plain meaning is simply this: you and Christ have been joined so deeply that His life is now the root of yours. You did not achieve it; it was given. Before you reconnect to anything else, before you fix a single thing, hear the secret Paul kept circling. You are already inhabited.

upheaval.thePhase: Reconnect begins here, at the deepest root. Reorientation found the new bearings; now the soul sinks down into the One who was the point of all of them. Paul names the mystery from his cell: Christ in you. Re-rooting is not first about rejoining a community or relearning a creed. It is discovering that the living Christ has made the interior of your life His home, and that everything else in this phase grows from that single root.
upheaval.inYou: After all the rebuilding, this is the anchor under the rest: not Christ as a distant authority, not Christ as a companion who walks beside you, but Christ in you. The whole journey cleared the ground for exactly this re-rooting. Your hope of glory is not your performance or even your recovered faith; it is the living Christ taking up residence in the actual interior of your ordinary life. Before you reconnect to anything else, know you are already inhabited.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church can hand people everything except the one thing that matters. Programs, belonging, sound teaching, a full calendar, and still never point them inward to the Christ who lives there. Paul says the mystery plainly: Christ in you. A community whose central work is helping people find the indwelling Christ, not merely join an organization, re-roots them where it counts. All the belonging in the world stays hollow without the One who has come to live inside.
upheaval.whatRemains: Roles can be stripped, certainties can crack, and even your felt faith can go quiet for a season. What cannot be shaken is the union itself, Christ joined to you so deeply that His life has become the root of yours. He did not move in on the condition that you keep performing, and He does not move out when you falter. He is in you. That is the ground.
reflection: Do I picture Christ mostly above me supervising, or beside me accompanying, rather than living within me?
What am I actually staking my hope of glory on right now, my performance or the indwelling Christ?
If I truly believed I were already inhabited, what striving could I finally lay down?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have looked everywhere for the secret, and all along it was nearer than my own breath. You are not above me keeping score, nor merely beside me for a while. You are in me. Let that union be the root I grow from now. Quiet my striving with the plain truth that I am already inhabited, and that You are my hope of glory. Amen.

notes.primary: Colossians 1:27 (Christ in you, the hope of glory); John 17:23 (I in them, and you in me).

title: You are inhabited
moment: For a thousand years there was one room on earth where the presence of God was said to settle, the holy of holies, deep inside the temple in Jerusalem, sealed off behind a heavy veil. No one entered but the high priest, and only once a year, and only with blood and trembling. The presence lived there, behind the curtain, in the dark, untouchable. Hold that picture, and then hear what Paul writes to a quarreling, ordinary, far-from-perfect church in Corinth, the kind of people who would never have been let near that inner room. Your body, he says, is a temple of the Holy Spirit. Not a building down the road. Not a sanctuary you visit on the holy day. You. The Spirit of the God who raised Jesus from the dead has not dropped by for a visit; He has moved in, settled down, taken up residence in the plain clay of a human life. The veil is not merely torn. The presence has relocated. After a season when you may have felt emptied of God, forsaken, scraped hollow, this is the re-rooting truth that resets everything. The holy of holies has an address now, and the address is you.
voiceQuote: Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God.
scriptureText: But if the Spirit of him who raised up Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised up Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you.
weight: In the worst of the upheaval you may have felt utterly empty of God, as if He had withdrawn and left a hollow where He used to be. Hear, then, where He actually is. The Spirit dwells in you. Indwelling is a large word for a simple, staggering fact: the Holy Spirit, God Himself, lives inside you, making your ordinary body the temple where His presence settles. He is not a visitor who comes and goes with your moods, present on the good days and gone on the bad. He took up permanent residence, and residence does not pack its bags when you feel nothing. Consider whose Spirit this is. The very Spirit who raised Jesus out of the grave now lives in you, and the same power that rolled the stone away will one day give life to your mortal body too. So when the emptiness whispers that you were abandoned, answer it with the truer word. You were not abandoned. The presence that once hid behind a veil now keeps house in you. You are inhabited.

upheaval.thePhase: Reconnect insists the Spirit does not visit and leave; He stays. After Corinth's chaos and your own, Paul relocates the holy of holies from a sealed inner room into the clay of a human life. Re-rooting here is the discovery that you are not a spectator waiting for a distant presence on the holy day, but a temple, consecrated, inhabited, the dwelling re-made. The presence that once hid behind a veil now lives in you, and means to stay.
upheaval.inYou: In the worst of it you may have felt emptied of God entirely. Hear where He actually is: the Spirit dwells in you, your body a temple, the holy presence relocated from a far-off sanctuary into the clay of your own life. He is no visitor who comes and goes with your moods; He has taken up permanent residence. The very Spirit who raised Jesus lives in you and will one day raise you too. You are not abandoned. You are inhabited.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church can speak of God as far off, met only in special rooms or on peak Sundays, leaving its people feeling like outsiders to the presence. Paul relocates the temple: the Spirit dwells in His people, each of them and all of them together. A community that treats its people as inhabited temples, carriers of the living God rather than spectators waiting on a distant presence, re-roots them in a startling dignity. The holy of holies is not down the road.
upheaval.whatRemains: Feelings of God can drain away, and a whole season can pass with the sanctuary seeming dark and empty. What cannot be shaken is the residence itself: the Spirit who raised Jesus has moved into you for good, and a resident does not leave when the lights feel low. He dwells, and the same power that emptied a tomb will one day fill your dust with life.
reflection: When did I last feel emptied of God, and what would change if I believed the Spirit never actually left?
Do I treat the Spirit as a visitor I must coax back, or as a resident who has settled in to stay?
What part of my ordinary life have I assumed is too common to be a temple of the living God?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have stood outside the veil so long I forgot You tore it down and moved in. When I felt hollow, You were not gone; You had taken up residence in this plain clay. Thank You that Your Spirit dwells in me and does not pack His bags when I feel nothing. Let the same power that raised Jesus quiet my fear of being abandoned, for I am inhabited by You. Amen.

notes.primary: 1 Corinthians 6:19 (your body, a temple of the Holy Spirit); Romans 8:11 (the Spirit who raised Jesus dwells in you).

title: Abba, Father
moment: There is a word a small child uses before the child knows any grand titles, before reverence or formality, the first warm sound for the one who lifts and holds and comes when called. In Jesus' own language the word was Abba, closer to Papa than to anything ceremonial. And Paul, writing to believers in Rome, says this is the very word the Spirit teaches a reconnected heart to cry. Picture the two postures he sets side by side. On the one hand, a servant who is unsure of his standing, hovering at the edge of the room, careful with his words, never quite certain he still has a place in the house. On the other, a child who runs across that same room and climbs straight into a parent's lap, wanting nothing, proving nothing, simply belonging there. You did not receive a spirit of slavery that drags you back to fear, Paul writes; you received the Spirit of adoption. And the legal weight of that word is enormous. To be adopted in the Roman world was to be made a full heir, the slave's status erased entirely, the new name real and permanent. After a long season of feeling like an outsider, an outsider even to God, the relationship is restored at its most intimate. Not a servant on probation. A child.
voiceQuote: You received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, Abba! Father!
scriptureText: So you are no longer a bondservant, but a son; and if a son, then an heir of God through Christ.
weight: If the upheaval left you feeling like an outsider, even with God, hovering at the edge as if you were not sure you still belonged, hear the word the Spirit is putting in your mouth. Abba. Not the careful address of a servant unsure whether he still has a job, weighing every syllable, braced to be dismissed, but the unguarded cry of a child climbing into a parent's lap. This is adoption, and the plain meaning is freeing: God has not taken you on as a worker on trial; He has made you His own child, with the full standing of one born into the family. You did not receive a spirit that drags you back into fear. You received the Spirit of adoption, the very life of God teaching you to come close. So you are no longer a servant on probation, anxious about your performance review. You are a son, a daughter, a full heir of everything that is His, and an heir does not earn the inheritance; he simply belongs to the family. Come close. The fear that kept you at the door was never the truth about you. Climb in, and call Him Abba.

upheaval.thePhase: Reconnect restores the relationship at its most intimate, not as a servant earning his keep but as an adopted child. Paul names the shift: out of a spirit of slavery and fear, into the Spirit of adoption that cries Abba. Re-rooting here means the security of a full heir replacing the nervousness of staff who fear dismissal. After feeling like an outsider even to God, the soul is brought all the way in, given the child's word and the child's place.
upheaval.inYou: If the upheaval left you feeling like an outsider even with God, hear the word the Spirit puts in your mouth: Abba. Not the cautious address of a servant unsure whether he still has a job, but the unguarded cry of a child climbing into a parent's lap. You did not receive a spirit that drags you back to fear; you received the Spirit of adoption. You are no longer a servant on probation but a son, a daughter, a full heir. Come close, and call Him Abba.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church can train people, without ever meaning to, to relate to God like anxious staff, forever unsure of their standing, working to stay employed, braced for the day they are let go. Paul names the truer relationship: adopted children crying Abba, full heirs by grace. A community that helps its people relate to God as beloved children rather than nervous servants re-roots them in intimacy. The household of God does not run on the fear of dismissal but on the security of adoption.
upheaval.whatRemains: Your performance will rise and fall, and on the low days the old fear will tell you that you have lost your place. What cannot be shaken is the adoption: a child made an heir is not un-childed by a bad week, and the family name, once given, is not revoked. You are not staff on trial. You are a son, a daughter, brought all the way in, and the inheritance was never wages you had to earn.
reflection: Do I come to God like a servant unsure of his standing, or like a child climbing into a lap?
Where is the spirit of fear still telling me I am on probation with God?
What in me struggles to believe that I am a full heir by gift, with nothing of the slave left?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, for too long I have hovered at the edge of the room, weighing my words, afraid I had lost my place in Your house. Thank You that You did not hire me as a servant on trial but adopted me as Your own child. Teach my heart the word the Spirit gives, Abba, and let me climb in close. I am no longer a slave to fear, but Your son, Your daughter, a full heir by grace. Amen.

notes.primary: Romans 8:15 (the Spirit of adoption, crying Abba, Father); Galatians 4:7 (no longer a slave but a son and heir).

title: Hidden with Christ
moment: Imagine the most secure vault you can picture, deep underground, thick steel, every wall built to keep one precious thing beyond the reach of any thief or fire or flood. The thing inside is not lost. It is not gone. It is hidden, kept, safe. Now hear what Paul tells the Colossians about the truest thing about you: you died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. The upheaval, you know too well, has a way of stripping things off, roles you wore, certainties you leaned on, a reputation, the old confident self you thought was the real you. The storm reached all of it, because all of it was on the surface, exposed to the weather. But the deepest you, your real life, was never out there where the wind could get to it. It was hidden, with Christ, in God, layered safe behind the One the shaking cannot touch. The psalmist sang of the same shelter long before: You are my hiding place; You will preserve me from trouble. There is a particular relief in this discovery, one that comes only on the far side of loss. What matters most about you was secured, all along, in the one place the storm could never reach.
voiceQuote: You died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.
scriptureText: You are my hiding place. You will preserve me from trouble. You will surround me with songs of deliverance.
weight: The upheaval stripped away a great deal you assumed was essential to you, the roles, the labels, the confident old self, and it can leave you feeling thinned out, scraped down to less than you were. Here is the relief Paul holds out. Your truest life was never on the exposed surface where the storm does its work. It is hidden with Christ in God. To be hidden here does not mean lost or forgotten; it means kept, the way something irreplaceable is locked in the one vault no thief can crack. Your deepest identity has been secured in Christ, layered behind the very life of God, beyond the reach of anything that shakes the surface of a life. So you may feel diminished, and on the surface perhaps you genuinely are, smaller than you were before the loss. But the deepest you is not diminished. It is safe, kept, hidden in God, and the psalmist says you are even now surrounded with songs of deliverance, sung over the part of you the storm could never get to. What was hidden in God cannot be plundered by what merely scours the surface.

upheaval.thePhase: Reconnect includes a deep, quiet relief: the discovery that your truest life was kept safe the whole time. Paul says you died, and your life is now hidden with Christ in God. Re-rooting here is not adding something new but uncovering what was always secured. The storm could reach the surface, the roles and the reputation, but never the deepest self, which was hidden beyond its reach. Reconnection finds that the real you was held safe where the shaking could not come.
upheaval.inYou: The upheaval stripped away much you thought was essential, the roles, the labels, the old confident self. Here is the relief: your truest life was never on the exposed surface. It is hidden with Christ in God, locked in the one vault the storm cannot reach. You may feel diminished, scraped down to less than you were. But the deepest you is not diminished; it is kept, safe, hidden in God, surrounded even now with songs of deliverance.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church can teach people to locate their identity in visible things, position, performance, reputation, applause, all of which a storm can strip away in a season. Paul points deeper: the real life of the believer is hidden with Christ in God, untouchable. A community that roots its people there, rather than in fragile surfaces, gives them a security no upheaval can plunder. What is hidden in God cannot be taken by what only shakes the surface.
upheaval.whatRemains: The surface of a life can be scoured down to almost nothing, the roles gone, the reputation spent, the old self unrecognizable. What cannot be shaken is the life kept in the vault: your truest self, hidden with Christ in God, beyond the reach of any storm. The shaking works only on the surface. The deepest you was secured before the trouble began, and it is secured still.
reflection: What did the upheaval strip from my surface, and have I mistaken that loss for the loss of my truest self?
Can I believe that the deepest me is hidden with Christ in God, beyond what any storm can reach?
Where am I still anchoring my identity to fragile, surface things the shaking can take?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, the storm reached so much I thought was me, and I have felt scraped down to almost nothing. Thank You that my truest life was never on the surface where the wind could get to it, but hidden with Christ in You, kept safe in the one place the shaking cannot reach. Quiet my fear of being diminished. You are my hiding place, and You surround even now with songs of deliverance. Amen.

notes.primary: Colossians 3:3 (your life is hidden with Christ in God); Psalm 32:7 (you are my hiding place).

title: Rooted and grounded in love
moment: Two trees stand in the same field when the dry year comes. The sun beats down the same on both, the rain holds off from both, the heat presses in from every side without favoring either one. But watch what happens as the drought drags on. The first tree, whose roots never went down far, browns at the edges, curls, drops its leaves, gives up its fruit; it lived off the surface, and the surface has failed it. The second tree seems hardly to notice the year at all. Its leaves stay green, it keeps setting fruit, because long before the heat ever came it sent its roots down and out, deep and patient, until they reached the river that runs underground where no drought reaches. Jeremiah draws that very picture: a tree planted by the waters, spreading its roots by the river, that will not fear when heat comes. And Paul names what the river is for the soul. Be rooted and grounded in love, he prays, with the love of Christ dwelling deep in your heart. This is the whole aim toward which the reconnecting season has been bending. Not a tree the heat will never touch. A tree whose roots have gone down far enough that the heat cannot win.
voiceQuote: that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith... being rooted and grounded in love.
scriptureText: For he will be as a tree planted by the waters, who spreads out its roots by the river, and will not fear when heat comes, but its leaf will be green, and will not cease from yielding fruit.
weight: You cannot promise yourself the heat will never come again. Droughts return; that is simply true, and pretending otherwise only sets you up to break. What you can do, in this season, is sink your roots. Paul prays that you would be rooted and grounded in love, that Christ would dwell deep in your heart, until you become like Jeremiah's tree by the river, green in the heat, fruitful in the drought, because your roots have quietly found the water that runs underground. To be rooted and grounded simply means to grow your life down into the love of God until that love, and not your circumstances, is what holds you up. This is the point of the whole reconnecting season, and it is gentler and more realistic than the promise you might have wished for. Not a life with no more hard summers. A root system deep enough to outlast them. So give yourself, now, in the watered season, to going deep, because roots are grown before the drought, not during it. Sink them into His love while the river is near, and when the heat comes again, and it will, your leaf will stay green.

upheaval.thePhase: Reconnect comes to its signature image here: roots driven so deep into the love of God that the next drought cannot finish you. Jeremiah's tree by the river does not fear the heat, because it found the water underground long before. Paul prays you would be rooted and grounded in love, with Christ dwelling deep in your heart. Re-rooting is exactly this, not a faith that escapes all heat, but one rooted deep enough that when the heat returns, the leaf stays green.
upheaval.inYou: You cannot guarantee the heat will not come again; droughts return. What you can do is sink your roots. Paul prays you would be rooted and grounded in love, with Christ dwelling deep in your heart, until you are like Jeremiah's tree by the river, green in the heat, fruitful in the drought, because your roots have found the water underground. This is the point of the whole reconnecting season: not a life without heat, but a root system deep enough to outlast it.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church can produce shallow-rooted believers who flourish in good seasons and brown at the first real heat, mistaking busy surface growth for depth. The aim Paul prays for is deeper: people rooted and grounded in the love of Christ, like trees planted by the river. A community devoted to sending roots down, into God's love and not merely into activity, raises people who stay green when the drought comes. Depth, not the absence of heat, is what holds.
upheaval.whatRemains: The heat will come again; no faith is promised a field without summers. What cannot be shaken is the river the roots have found, the love of Christ that runs deeper than any drought and does not dry up when the surface does. A tree rooted there stays green not because the heat spares it, but because its roots reached water the heat cannot touch. The love holds when nothing else does.
reflection: Am I waiting for a life without heat, or growing roots deep enough to outlast the heat when it comes?
How deep have my roots actually gone into the love of God, beneath my changing circumstances?
What would it look like, in this watered season, to sink roots now rather than scramble for them in the next drought?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I would love a field with no more dry summers, but You offer something better and truer. Root me and ground me in Your love. Let Christ dwell so deep in my heart that my roots reach the river that runs beneath every drought. I cannot keep the heat from coming, but You can hold me green within it. Sink me down into Your love while the water is near. Amen.

notes.primary: Ephesians 3:17 (rooted and grounded in love); Jeremiah 17:8 (a tree planted by the waters, unafraid of heat).

title: As the deer pants
moment: The deer has been on the move for days. The streambeds it knows are cracked clay; the hill grass has gone to straw. It does not reason about water, it simply aches toward it, ears up, nostrils wide, every nerve bent toward the one thing it lacks. Then, far off, on the moving air, the faint cool scent of a brook still out of sight. The animal breaks into a run it has no strength for, drawn by thirst alone, and when it finally reaches the water it drops its head and drinks as though its life hangs on it, because it does. The sons of Korah watched some creature like this and saw their own souls in it. As the deer pants for the water brooks, they sang, so my soul pants after you, God. What strikes you is not the drinking but the panting that comes first, the longing before the finding. In a dry and weary land where there is no water, the very thirst is the proof that something in them was still alive and still aimed at God. The ache itself had become the early sign that the long drought was breaking.
voiceQuote: As the deer pants for the water brooks, so my soul pants after you, God.
scriptureText: God, you are my God. I will earnestly seek you. My soul thirsts for you, my flesh longs for you, in a dry and weary land where there is no water.
weight: Somewhere in the worst of it, you may have stopped wanting God at all. Not rebellion, exactly, just a dryness so complete that even the thirst went quiet, and you no longer reached for Him because reaching had begun to seem pointless. So watch closely for the first thing to come back, because it is rarely fullness. It is longing. One ordinary day you notice your soul beginning to pant after God again, thirsting, leaning, aching toward Him in a land that is still dry. Do not despise that ache as weakness, and do not wait to feel satisfied before you trust it. The waking desire is itself the mercy, the deer catching the scent of water it has not yet reached. The thirst is not the absence of grace; it is grace arriving early, in the only form a parched soul can receive it. He is the one who put the wanting back. Follow it the way the deer follows the scent on the wind, and let it carry you, still thirsty, toward the brook.

upheaval.thePhase: Reconnect does not always begin with God felt, satisfied, near. Often it begins with God wanted again. The sons of Korah sing the early stage of it: a soul panting, thirsting, longing in a dry land, the desire itself coming back to life before the water is reached. Re-rooting starts here, in a reawakened ache. Where the drought had killed even the wanting, the returning thirst is the first green shoot.
upheaval.inYou: Notice if your soul has begun, quietly, to want God again. After a season when even the longing dried up, that ache is not a sign you are failing; it is a sign you are reviving. Do not wait for fullness to believe He is near. The thirst is the deer catching the scent of the brook on the wind, and the One who set that scent moving is already drawing you toward the water. Let the wanting lead.
upheaval.inTheBody: Many gatherings prize a settled, satisfied look and quietly teach people to perform contentment, mistaking dry duty for devotion. But the psalms model a soul that pants and thirsts out loud. A community brave enough to let people name their spiritual thirst, to long for God without pretending the brook is already reached, nurtures the realer thing. The honest ache for God, shared, is nearer to true worship than a tidy contentment that has stopped desiring Him.
upheaval.whatRemains: Feelings of nearness rise and fall, and there are seasons when even the longing seems to die. What the drought cannot finally kill is the thirst God Himself planted, the ache He keeps reviving in souls made for Him. When you find yourself wanting Him again, you are touching the one desire no wilderness can dry out for good.
reflection: When did I last notice a genuine thirst for God, and did I treat it as weakness or as mercy?
Am I waiting to feel full before I will trust Him, when the longing itself may be the gift?
What would it mean to follow my reawakened desire toward God rather than despising it?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, for a long while I did not even want You, and the thirst itself had dried up in me. Thank You that the wanting is coming back. I will not despise this ache. I see now it is the early water, the scent of the brook on the wind, Your mercy reaching me before the fullness does. Draw me, still thirsty, all the way to Yourself. Amen.

notes.primary: Psalm 42:1 (the deer panting for water, the soul for God); Psalm 63:1 (my soul thirsts for you).

title: The secret place
figure: The shelter of the Most High
moment: The storm came up the valley faster than anyone climbing the ridge could outrun it, and the wind drove the rain sideways across the bare rock. But the face of the cliff was not smooth. A little higher, a deep cleft cut back into the stone, an angle the weather could not turn, and a person who reached it could press in out of the wind and, for the first time in hours, stop bracing. The shoulders come down. The clenched body unlocks. Inside the cleft, the storm is still audible, still raging a few feet away, but it cannot reach in. The psalmist knew a shelter like that and made it a picture of God. He who dwells in the secret place of the Most High, he wrote, will rest in the shadow of the Almighty. Listen to the verb he chose. Not he who visits the secret place, who drops by in emergencies, but he who dwells there, who has made it home. There is a hidden place, the psalm insists, an interior shelter the wreckage of a whole upheaval cannot follow you into, where the bracing finally stops and a soul learns, again, to rest.
voiceQuote: He who dwells in the secret place of the Most High will rest in the shadow of the Almighty.
scriptureText: I will say of the LORD, He is my refuge and my fortress; my God, in whom I trust.
weight: You may have come through the upheaval with your beliefs eventually patched back together and still have no resting place in God. That is the difference this psalm presses. Reconnection is more than getting your theology back in order; it is recovering a hidden, interior place where you actually meet Him and let yourself rest. You have likely forgotten the way there, or assumed the storm collapsed it for good. It did not. The cleft in the rock is still cut into the stone, still angled against the wind, still yours. So slip away to it. Not to fix anything, not to perform, not to brace against the next blow, but simply to dwell, to be sheltered, to stop. Say it slowly, as your own and not just the psalmist's: the Lord is my refuge and my fortress, my God, in whom I trust. The noise of the world cannot follow you in. Stop visiting God in passing crises and learn again to live in the shelter, where the storm is real but no longer reaches you.

upheaval.thePhase: Reconnect is not finished when the doctrines are sorted; it is underway when the soul finds shelter again. The psalmist points past public religion to a secret place of the Most High, a hidden intimacy where one dwells, not merely visits, and rests in God's shadow. Re-rooting means recovering that interior cleft in the rock, the sheltered place the long storm could not reach, where you finally stop bracing and learn once more to abide.
upheaval.inYou: You can have your beliefs back and still be braced for the next blow. Find your way again to the interior shelter, the cleft in the rock where the storm is loud but cannot reach in. You have not lost it; you have only forgotten the path. Go there not to fix yourself but to rest. Let your shoulders come down. The secret place is still there, and it is still yours.
upheaval.inTheBody: A community can fill people's calendars with public devotion and never help them recover a private, sheltered life with God. The psalm names a secret place, an interior refuge where the soul dwells and rests. A gathering that teaches its people to seek that hidden shelter, and not only to attend and perform, re-roots them in a place the world cannot invade. All the public worship is hollow without the secret place beneath it holding it up.
upheaval.whatRemains: Storms keep coming, and public religion can carry on long after the inner rest has gone. What the weather cannot reach is the secret place itself, the shelter in God that no upheaval can collapse. The cleft was cut before your storm and stands after it. You may have forgotten the way in, but the refuge never stopped being there.
reflection: Have I mistaken patched-up beliefs for the deeper rest of actually dwelling with God?
Where am I still braced against the next blow instead of sheltering in the secret place?
What would it look like for me to go to God this week simply to rest, and not to fix or perform?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have been braced so long that I forgot how to rest. I have visited You in emergencies and called it dwelling. Lead me back into the secret place, the cleft in the rock where the storm cannot reach, and teach me to stop bracing. You are my refuge and my fortress, my God, in whom I trust. Let me live in the shelter again. Amen.

notes.primary: Psalm 91:1 (dwelling in the secret place of the Most High); Psalm 91:2 (the LORD my refuge and fortress).

title: Like a weaned child
moment: A baby in arms cries when it is hungry, and nothing but the feeding will quiet it; the whole small body strains toward the one thing it wants. But there is an older child, just weaned, who has learned something the infant has not. Carried against the mother now, this child is not fretting to be fed. It has discovered that she is simply there, that her nearness is itself the thing, and so it rests against her shoulder wanting nothing she has to give, only her. The grasping has stilled. The body, once all reaching, has gone quiet and heavy with trust. David, a king who had every reason to keep striving, reaches for exactly this image to describe what had happened in his soul. I have stilled and quieted my soul, he sings, like a weaned child with his mother. Not a soul that got everything it demanded, but a soul that stopped demanding, that learned to want the Presence more than the provision. The frantic grasping had eased, and something rarer had taken its place: a soul content, at last, simply to be held.
voiceQuote: I have stilled and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with his mother.
scriptureText: My soul rests in God alone. My salvation is from him.
weight: Even on the far side of the upheaval, your soul can stay frantic. You may have your faith back and still be clutching at God, needing Him to prove Himself by producing, to fix the situation, to deliver the outcome, to justify the trust by performing on schedule. David shows a quieter country. He stilled his soul like a weaned child, content simply to be held, no longer crying to be fed. Let your striving settle into that. You are allowed to rest in God alone, to want His presence more than His gifts, to stop measuring His love by what He hands you. The grasping eases the moment you discover what your soul was actually after all along. It was never the provision in His hands. It was Him. And He has not withheld Himself; He is already here, holding you, while you learn to stop clamoring and simply lean your weight on Him.

upheaval.thePhase: Reconnect is not only believing again; it is being quieted. After the upheaval the soul can keep grasping, still demanding that God produce. David models the further thing: a soul stilled and quieted like a weaned child, content with the mother's presence, not crying to be fed. Re-rooting brings this settling. The frantic reaching eases, and the soul learns to rest in God alone, wanting the One who holds it more than anything held in His hands.
upheaval.inYou: Notice the grasping, even now. You may have your faith back and still be clutching at God to fix, to prove, to deliver on demand. David points to a stiller place: a soul quieted like a weaned child, content to be held, no longer crying to be fed. Let your striving settle. You can rest in God alone, wanting His presence more than His gifts, once you discover that being with Him, not what He produces, was the thing your soul was after.
upheaval.inTheBody: A community can keep its people in a perpetual fret, forever striving, always measuring God by results delivered. David shows a quieted soul, weaned of the frantic grasping, resting in God alone. A gathering that helps its people stop performing and simply be with God, content in His presence rather than clamoring for outcomes, re-roots them in rest. The stilled soul, not the restless and demanding one, is the soul that has actually reconnected.
upheaval.whatRemains: Circumstances stay tangled, and God does not always hand you the outcome you came clutching for.
